utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Banbury. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, members of the Trial Chamber. I would just like to introduce one of our legal interns who is with us this morning. Her name is Julia Kretzenbacher, and she's from Melbourne University. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Banbury. Could you actually state your full name for us, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Anthony Nathan Banbury.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Banbury, in 1997 you gave a statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor here at this Tribunal on your observations and your experiences while you served with the United Nations as part of UNPROFOR in the former Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in 2009, do you recall meeting me, together with a colleague of mine, and giving a further statement incorporating, clarifying and augmenting that statement from 1997?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that 2009 statement referred to a number of documents that weren't available at the time the first statement was recorded; is that not the case?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And have you looked at that 2009 statement, as well as those documents, in preparation for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any corrections or further clarifications you wanted to make as a result of that review?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I was to ask you the same questions today as those that gave rise to the evidence set out in the 2009 statement, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, materially, the answers would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 2009 statement is 65 ter 22657. Could that be marked as a Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2451, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now read a summary of the written evidence in P2451. Anthony Banbury served with the United Nations in the former Yugoslavia from April 1994 until the end of the conflict. He was first a Civil Affairs officer in UNPROFOR Headquarters Sarajevo until 1 May 1995. Then he worked as an assistant to the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, Mr. Yasushi Akashi. In both roles, Mr. Banbury attended meetings with leaders of the warring factions and drafted reports, cables, letters and other correspondence on behalf of his superiors. Mr. Banbury states that the population in Sarajevo suffered because of a constant campaign of shelling and sniping that was directed at civilians. He observed that: "The weaponry employed, particularly mortars and sniping, meant that no matter where you lived, as soon as you stepped outside, you could be killed at any moment." From attending frequent meetings with the Bosnian Serb leadership, Mr. Banbury observed that they were able to modulate conditions in Sarajevo by controlling the supply of utilities, the freedom of movement, and the level of shelling and sniping, among other things. In April 1995, for example, the accused, Dr. Karadzic, announced that he had closed the airport in Sarajevo to "show the world who was in control of the airport." Mr. Banbury states that in meetings attended by the Bosnian Serb leadership, the accused was clearly in control, and he was alone in straddling both the political and military spheres of the leadership. He demonstrated his control by negotiating and entering into agreements on a range of matters. On occasion, the accused expressed concern about being dominated by the Muslims in Bosnia. At a dinner in April 1995, he said that Serbs had lived with Muslims for 500 years and, quote: "... no more. The same in Cyprus and India. Hindus were very tolerant, but they can't live with Muslims." The accused was frequently provided with notice of crimes being committed by Serb forces during the course of meetings with UN representatives. For example, at the same dinner in April, the force commander, General Janvier, complained to Dr. Karadzic that Serb forces targeted civilian targets. The accused joked in reply that: "Maybe some of our gunners have bad eyes." That's the end of the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Banbury, before we go into some more detail about your written evidence that's just been filed, I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about your personal background, and that's at paragraphs 2 to 4 of your 2009 statement. And my first question is: Your work with UNPROFOR wasn't actually your first job with the United Nations, was it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: No. I had worked in three previous capacities for the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what were those?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I served for approximately two years as a human rights protection officer, working in refugee camps on the Thai-Cambodian border for the United Nations border relief operation. That was 1988 to 1990. I served as a human rights officer in the United Nations peacekeeping operation in Cambodia from 1992 to 1993, about a year and a half. And I served briefly in the UN OAS, Organisation of American States, joint mission in Haiti as a human rights officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, since giving this statement that you gave in 2009, when you served as the World Food Programme's regional director for Asia, you've actually since returned to the United Nations, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Well, the World Food Programme technically is a part of the United Nations, but I've moved to -- I've returned to the United Nations headquarters in a new job, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what's that new job?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Right now, I am serving as the United Nations assistant secretary-general for field support. That is a department that provides all the operational and logistic support to UN peacekeeping missions and special political missions around the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to jump back again to your time with UNPROFOR, I wonder if you could outline for us what your main tasks were, first working with Civil Affairs and then working for Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I was deployed to Sarajevo at the very beginning of April 1994; April 9th, I believe. And normally Civil Affairs officers, when they are first in the mission, would be deployed to a small town somewhere or a city to serve in a regional capacity, but the head of the UN civilian operation in Bosnia, UNPROFOR civilian operation, Mr. Andreev, decided to attach me to his immediate staff and serve essentially as a political officer for him, together with mainly one other person. And in that role, I -- I was essentially an assistant or political advisor to the head civilian of UNPROFOR. I attended meetings with him with the different parties to the conflict, with representatives of member states who would visit, ministers, ambassadors, et cetera. I routinely prepared him for the meetings and then routinely wrote a summary of the different meetings; normally, a factual accounting of the main points that were discussed in the meetings, the main positions of the different sides. And then, normally, some kind of assessment or analysis at the end of the report so that our superiors in Zagreb and New York would have not just an accounting of what had transpired in the meeting, but our best assessment of the significance of that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did that function change when you moved to work for Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes. In my role in Bosnia, I was limited just to working on Bosnia issues. I regularly met with the -- or together with Mr. Andreev, my boss, we'd meet with heads of the different parties to the conflict, but only in Bosnia, the Bosnian parties. When I moved to Zagreb in May 1995, May 1, 1995, I became special assistant to Mr. Akashi, and in that role the function was very similar, but it incorporated the entire territory where UNPROFOR was working, so also quite a lot of responsibilities in Zagreb and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, when you say you met with the heads of the different parties to the conflict, first of all, in Bosnia, who were these people, who were Mr. Andreev's interlocutors during these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic, Mr. Silajdzic, Mr. Muratovic, Mr. Ganic, on the Bosnian Government side. On the Bosnian Serb side, Mr. Andreev and I routinely met with Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Professor Koljevic, General Mladic, General Gvero, General Tolimir. Those were our main interlocutors, and then also some on the Bosnian Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you moved then to meet with Mr. -- or to work with Mr. Akashi, did you continue to meet with these interlocutors on the Bosnian and Bosnian Serb sides?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I did, though not as frequently because I was based in Zagreb instead of Sarajevo. So I would only meet with them when Mr. Akashi would travel. In the past, it was -- the meetings were very frequent. They were less frequent with Mr. Akashi. But then I was also meeting with President Tudjman, President Milosevic, and some of their senior officials.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the meetings you had with these interlocutors, what other sources of information did you rely on in preparing your superiors for the meetings, in preparing your assessments, your analyses? What did you have available to you, and what did you rely on?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Well, my superiors would also frequently meet with officials of member states of the United Nations, either resident ambassadors or visiting ministers. There were very often high-level visits from key member states. And those discussions inevitably were quite political and gave an indication of where that particular member state stood or how they saw the conflict or the UN role. In addition, we had a service in UNPROFOR in Sarajevo that listened to or collected information from all the local media from the different parties, translated it, and provided that assessment to us or a summary to us. The local media was a hugely important source of information for us, both factual information, what was happening in different parts of the country, but also more giving us a sense of the political aims of the parties, where they saw the conflict headed, how they saw their role, how they saw the role of the other parties to the conflict. And we lived this war day in and day out. We were always talking about it. We were always talking about, among ourselves, what was happening, what the significance of events were, what the significance of statements were. We were immersed in it and had information coming from -- information and analysis coming from just a range of sources, talking to local people that we knew. And over time, I think, there were a few people in UNPROFOR who developed quite a good understanding of what was happening in the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did your sources include, for example, other humanitarian organisations, the Red Cross, UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes. The UNPROFOR headquarters, what we called Bosnia-Herzegovina Command Forward based in Sarajevo, which was the headquarters for the UNPROFOR lead general for Bosnia, at the time General Rose, later General Smith, as well as the lead civilian, Mr. Andreev for most of the time I was there, it was kind of a centre in Sarajevo. We constantly were receiving visitors, whether it was from member states or different UN organisations, UNHCR, ICRC, different NGOs. They were always streaming through there, wanting to meet with us, talk to us either about a specific issue or concern they might have or just in general to find out what was going on and share with us what was going on. So it was really almost a crossroads, in some senses. It was probably the most important stop for anyone coming through the city, and as a result we were able to meet with quite a wide array of officials -- civilian officials, military officials, aid workers, government officials. And as a result of that, we were able to learn the perspective of all those different actors.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what about UNPROFOR units on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: There was regular reporting coming in from the different UNPROFOR sector commands. They had to report daily to us what was happening. And, of course, if the sector commander came in to Sarajevo for any purpose, meetings, whatever, he would normally come in and see the political leadership as well as the military. We also had a daily briefing, a morning briefing, where the briefer would report based on the reports coming in from the different military units, as well as UN military observers, UN police. They would report to us, in the briefing, what was happening. They would give us a summary so we didn't necessarily have to read all the voluminous reports coming in. We were able to benefit from that daily briefing where they would summarise the most important events.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on to another topic now, something that you addressed in your written evidence, and that's Sarajevo. In your written evidence, at paragraph 197, in regard to Sarajevo, I see that you noted, and I'll quote. "The multi-ethnic traditions of Sarajevo were contrary to the objectives of the Bosnian Serb leadership." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if you could clarify this for us. Could you explain what you understood those objectives to be?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: My understanding of the Bosnian Serb war objectives were that they wanted to have or control or define certain territorial space in which they had total political control and in which Bosnian -- or Serbs could live separately from Muslims and Croats, and that this land should include the land where traditionally Serbs had lived in in Bosnia, even if other ethnic groups had also lived there. But wherever there were significant Serb populations before the war, they felt that those lands should be Serb lands, that the lands should be contiguous, should not be separated East and West Bosnia, but they needed a fairly wide corridor in the north to connect the two sides. And over that land, they wanted to exercise total political control.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Still in relation to Sarajevo, just a couple of paragraphs further in your evidence, you wrote that: "Karadzic and Mladic had the ability to modulate the level of terror caused by the campaign of shelling and sniping, and could improve conditions, for example -- by, for example, opening the airport, allowing commercial supplies, stopping shelling, stopping sniping, and equally make them worse by restricting things. Both men demonstrated such abilities by using them as leverage in negotiations." Now, in regard to that, I'd like to ask you how. How did they use these conditions, if I can call them that, the opening of the airport, allowing commercial supplies, stopping shelling, stopping sniping, how did they use them as leverage in negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I think they had three target groups, really. One was the population of Sarajevo, two was UNPROFOR, and three was the broader international community. And they tried to influence each one in different ways, though their -- the control that the Bosnian Serbs exerted over Sarajevo, including the airport, was a source where they could -- they could influence all three groups, really. They could, at their will, increase the level of sniping or mortar fire into the city or decrease it. They could, at their will and very quickly, expand the access of humanitarian assistance to the city or cut it off. They could, at their will and very quickly, expand UNPROFOR's access to and from the city or restrict it. The same for humanitarian organisations. And by -- through their ability to do that, to turn it on and off so quickly or modulate it, expand it a little, decrease it a little, decrease it a lot, they were able to exert influence, create leverage over us. When they would say, Block humanitarian access to the city, or, Limit UNPROFOR's ability to travel to enter or leave the city, that created pressure on us and a need for us to go negotiate with them and say, Please, let humanitarian convoys in, or, Open the airport so our troops can fly in or out. And they would say, Well, if you want us to do that, then you have to do this in return, or they would use that as leverage in the negotiations. And as a result, they were able to put UNPROFOR in the position of supplicant, having to constantly go beg for access, whether it was for us or for humanitarian organisations. They were able to hold the population of the city hostage, essentially, and they were able to pressure Security Council members, in particular; more broadly, the international community, but, in particular, Security Council members who didn't want to get wrapped up in a war in Bosnia. And if the Serbs were -- the Bosnian Serbs were threatening conflict if we didn't change our behaviour, I think that influenced the thinking of some Security Council members and Contact Group members.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just in terms of examples, you mentioned the airport as being one of those, and you also made that point in paragraph 66 of your written evidence. How were they able to control the operation of the airport?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: They were able to shut it down at their will by -- essentially, they would say, We can't guarantee the safety of flights coming in and out of the airport. And that was code for, you know, the planes are at risk, we can't guarantee their safety, they could be shot down. And without assurances of safety for the flights, they wouldn't fly. And at times, planes were shot at. Many times, our planes with hit by gun-fire. And in those conditions, the planes wouldn't fly or certain limitations would be put on them; only UN personnel could fly in or out, or no UN civilians could fly in or out. You know, it depended on the situation. They put various kinds of restrictions on us. They had personnel -- military personnel at the airport who would conduct inspections of the flights, and at any time they could -- or the cargo. And at any time, they could object to something and shut down our whole operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On what basis do you put, as you did in paragraph 200, Karadzic and Mladic as being the decision-makers in this regard?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic was the leader of the Bosnian Serbs and, in my view, the ultimate authority who made decisions on all major issues, the strategic issues, the important issues. Of course, many small issues never reached him, but on any significant issue, that's where we had to go to get a resolution. In the case of General Mladic, there were -- he was the head of the Bosnian Serb Army, the head of the Bosnian Serb military, so that's where we would go to get resolution of primarily military matters. General Mladic did not get involved, for the most part, in civilian matters, and -- but he was the ultimate -- or he was the main purely military authority. With Dr. Karadzic, as supreme commander, he had a role both in the civilian side as well as the military side. And if we couldn't get a resolution with Professor Koljevic on some humanitarian issue, or airport access issue, or with Mr. Krajisnik or with General Tolimir, we would go up the chain and eventually reach Dr. Karadzic or General Mladic if we couldn't get the issue resolved somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: While we're discussing this matter -- as we're discussing this, perhaps it's a good time to turn to one of the documents mentioned in your statement, and that's 65 ter 11172. It's an entry from your notebook of events that -- related to events that transpired on 24 April 1995. Do you see that on the screen in front of you, Mr. Banbury?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just in relation to your handwritten notes which are among these associated exhibits in your statement, could you just tell us: What was your practice in note-taking? How complete were your notes?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I would try and take as close to -- not verbatim notes as possible, but close to it. I would try and get down a lot of key quotes word for word; not for the whole meeting, but key statements, and really record as much of an entire meeting or event that was taking place as possible, avoiding the pleasantries and things like that. But all of the substantive conversation, I would try and get down either the complete meaning of it or, at times, verbatim quotes. So they were pretty comprehensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just, then, please, have a look at this excerpt. It's a two-page excerpt of events on 28 April, and perhaps you could put this excerpt in context for us. What was going on in and around Sarajevo at this time? Sorry, on 24 April, I meant to say. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: There had been a cessation of hostilities agreement in December 1994, December/January 1995, that had made -- that was signed by the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Government following President Carter's peace efforts in December 1994, and that Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, or COHA, had a big impact on the situation on the ground. Initially, the parties broadly respected their undertakings in the COHA. January 1995 was a good time in Sarajevo, and the COHA was meant to create an atmosphere in which more comprehensive peace talks could take place. It was meant to cool the situation on the ground so that peace talks could progress. And the COHA achieved its objectives in January, broadly speaking I would say, and to a large extent in February. The situation started to deteriorate around March, probably, because the peace talks that were supposed to take place were not progressing, really. And by April 1995, it was clear that the peace talks were going nowhere. And as a result, the concept behind the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement was -- the premise behind it was flawed, it was no longer operational, and the parties were returning to a military conflict, to pursuing their objectives through military means. And as a result, the situation in Sarajevo in April 1995 was pretty quickly deteriorating and was much worse than it had been in January.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go over to the second page of this excerpt, and if you could please magnify it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just under halfway down to the page -- or down the page, I see a reference to Dr. Karadzic, and the notation is: "Karadzic on VOA (not quoted)." Do you see that reference?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us, first of all, what "VOA" means? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Voice of America.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you, since it's your handwriting and you can interpret that better than all of us, read for us the passage that follows?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: It says: "The international community must accept Serb plans for peace or the Bosnian Serb Army will invade Sarajevo. Also, Dr. Karadzic said that he had closed the Sarajevo Airport over the weekend to show the world who was in control of the airport."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, first of all, then, is this consistent with the situation as regards control of the operation of the airport you've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall why -- or do you recall the situation which led to the closure of the airport by Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Their -- I believe it was the general deterioration in the situation in the city, and, as I said, people were -- or the sides were resorting more toward pursuing their aims through military means. I do not recall whether there was a specific incident that prompted it. There may have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask this be marked as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2452, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like us to talk about paragraph 32 of your written evidence, which contained a discussion regarding -- or of sniping, or on sniping. And before we do that in more detail, I wonder if you could tell us whether you, yourself, have actually seen sniping victims during your tour in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen a sniping victim in Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you describe what you saw?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: It was -- or she was an elderly woman who was killed by sniping in the area of the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 32 of your statement, there's -- the last line in paragraph 32 is a bit of a cumbersome sentence, where you say: "The argument that the military, including off-duty soldiers, were intermingled with the population, and therefore sniping was justified, is belied by the fact that civilians, including women, children and the elderly, were regularly victims of sniping." So, actually, in regard to this passage, perhaps you could give us a little bit of clarification. By this, do you mean to say that there were no military targets in Sarajevo at all?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: No, I don't mean to suggest that there were no military targets in Sarajevo. What I mean to say is that the preponderance of victims of sniping in Sarajevo were civilians. And sniping is not an indiscriminate weapon the way, say, mortars are. Or mortars are somewhat indiscriminate. Sniping is very targeted at a single individual. And the victims of sniping that UNPROFOR was concerned with, and the people who were routinely victims in Sarajevo, were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go on to another area that comes up on several occasions in your statement, and it's the subject of freedom of movement for the United Nations and other humanitarian organisations through Bosnian Serb-held territory. And perhaps I could ask you this: Were there areas of Bosnia, to your recollection, that were particularly reliant on the UN's delivery of aid?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Absolutely. I mean, Bosnia -- many civilians throughout Bosnia were wholly or largely reliant on humanitarian assistance from the UN or NGOs for their survival. So the population, as a whole, or large portions of the population were quite reliant on us for their survival, really. And there were some parts of the country where our ability to maintain that aid supply was wholly dependent upon Serb acquiescence to the continuation of that supply.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, what areas were those?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Well, the three main ones were the eastern enclaves, Srebrenica, Gorazde and Zepa. Sarajevo was largely reliant; not completely, but largely reliant. And Bihac, depending -- there were other groups through whom we had to get -- or whose co-operation we had to get for their supply. There were different routes into Bihac, but one was dependent upon the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did the United Nations then have freedom of movement to those areas you've just identified?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Well, legally, we did. The Security Council resolutions authorising UNPROFOR and giving us our mandate made it clear that it was a right to which we were entitled. It was an obligation of all the parties to the conflict. But, no, we never had real freedom of movement, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Because the -- in the case of the eastern enclaves, for instance, the Bosnian Serbs placed a range of restrictions on us. The degree to which we were able to access the areas that I previously mentioned varied, and sometimes the restrictions were less onerous and our ability to access these areas and provide humanitarian assistance to the population was -- our ability was greater, and we were able to, to a large degree, successfully carry out that responsibility, though many times our freedom of movement was greatly constrained, our ability to carry out our mandate in these areas was very limited, if not completely restricted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did those variations depend on anything in particular? How did they come about?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: They depended entirely on the position of the Bosnian Serb leadership in Pale, and they would impose different kinds of restrictions on us for different reasons. There were often links -- they linked their willingness to grant us access to different issues, and oftentimes there was no reasonable or logical link. They were using the -- our need to provide humanitarian assistance to people wholly dependent upon us, to resupply our troops, to rotate our troops, that was an absolute need for UNPROFOR. And since they totally controlled our ability to fulfil that need, they had great leverage over us. They oftentimes sought to use that leverage in other areas that were important to them, but not necessarily linked in any way to the issue of freedom of movement or access to the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, then maybe we could look at a further document, since you've raised that point. 65 ter 10628, and that's a report dated 15 December 1994 on a meeting with Bosnian Serb authorities on UNPROFOR freedom of movement. Do you see that document on the screen in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you're noted as being the drafter of that document?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the attendees at the meeting included you, the BH Command Chief of Staff, General Brinkman, Lieutenant-Colonel Daniell, the head of G3 convoy ops, and the Bosnian Serb representatives at the meeting were then Lieutenant-Colonel Tolimir and Major Indic. If we could turn to paragraph 3 -- pardon me, page 3 of this document, paragraph 5, I'd like to ask you a question. Now, here we see that significant progress was reported on the issue of freedom of movement, but the document says: "The willingness of Tolimir to make progress on our freedom of movement is no doubt linked to Dr. Karadzic's attempt to engage President Carter in the peace process. Were the BSA to fail to live up to their commitments, Karadzic's efforts would also fail. Our freedom of movement is once again being used by the BS," and I assume by that you mean Bosnian Serbs, "as a pawn in their political machinations, but at least this time the moves are in our favour." Now, is this consistent with the situation you've just been describing?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, it's a good example of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this be marked as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2453, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you commented on this document at the end of paragraph 95, saying: "Again, this is an example of Karadzic being able to turn the pressure on and off as he pleased." And I'd like to know on what basis you attribute this control of freedom of movement to Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: This meeting occurred at a very important time. It was following the fighting and crisis in Bihac in November and just before President Carter was arriving. And I think the Bosnian Government authorities were concerned by the Carter mission and that they would be placed under pressure to accept things they didn't want. I think the Bosnian Serb authorities were hopeful that the Carter mission would deliver to them things they did want. However, following the Bihac fighting and the use of air power by NATO, the Bosnian Serb authorities had responded in their traditional way, which was to -- they had a strategy, a quite good or intelligent strategy from their perspective, I suppose, to ensure that whenever UNPROFOR, in combination with NATO, used force, used air power, to achieve some Security Council mandated objective, they would exact a very high price from us and -- by shutting down freedom of movement, shutting down the airport, stopping humanitarian supplies from reaching the enclaves, et cetera. And as a result, they would ensure that they ended up in a strategically superior position to UNPROFOR following the use of force by UNPROFOR and/or NATO. They were willing to go further up the ladder of escalation than we were. And because of this strategy that they pursued, they created a big dis-incentive on the part of many to the use of force. It was a very effective strategy. This happened following the incidents in Bihac in November 1995, just prior to this meeting, so we were facing all kinds of restrictions, both in terms of delivery of humanitarian assistance and our own freedom of movement, and, of course, we were protesting this. We were travelling to Pale, asking for the restrictions to be lifted. We were in the role of supplicant following the use of force, and the Serbs were able to refuse all our entreaties. Then when the Carter mission was organised, I think it was understood by the Bosnian Serb authorities that they would come under a lot of pressure from President Carter, immediately upon his arrival, to deal with these other issues if they were outstanding, because they were so objectionable, they were so unjustified, putting these kind of restrictions on delivery of humanitarian assistance on the UN peacekeeping force. As a result, there was a quite rational political decision, I believe taken at the highest levels in Pale, to grant -- I'm hesitant to use the word "concession," though this was the way it was often created, given the strategic dynamic. Again, it was very clever. But the Bosnian Serb authorities decided to allow us greater freedom of movement, resumption of humanitarian supplies, et cetera, in order to come across as a more reasonable party, not the one that's imposing undue -- unwarranted restrictions on UNPROFOR. This was a very important political strategic decision, and I don't believe it could have been made by anyone other than Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've just touched on, a couple of times now, these restrictions on freedom of movement having an affect on UNPROFOR's operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I wonder, if you recall, was that also the case with respect to the eastern enclaves where UNPROFOR was stationed?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Those enclaves were the places where we were most vulnerable to restrictions on freedom of movement and where the issue -- that and Sarajevo, to an extent, but really the freedom of movement issue was most pronounced in terms of the eastern enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have, then, a look at another document, 65 ter 09686.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a report dated 19 November 1994, which you drafted, on a meeting with UNPROFOR -- of UNPROFOR military officials with Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and General Tolimir, and others. And I note, at the end of paragraph 1, one of the main topics of conversation is the near zero or zero levels of food and fuel for UNPROFOR troops in the eastern enclaves. I wonder, first of all, if I could ask you: Is this, to your mind, one of the results of the restrictions we've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we go over to paragraph 5 of this document, which I think I recall is on the next page in English. It begins, at paragraph 5 -- or it begins on the next page, bottom of the next page. We see there that Dr. Karadzic is recorded as eventually allowing food and fuel stocks for UNPROFOR for one week into the enclaves, and he noted that UNPROFOR -- if we go over to -- sorry. He noted that -- or it is noted that UNPROFOR's requirements are going to be determined by the Bosnian Serb Army headquarters, following submission by BH Command of your declared requirements "tomorrow." If we could go over to page 3, please, "tomorrow" being the next day. And at paragraph 6, General Brinkman reminds Dr. Karadzic of his agreement with the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on UNPROFOR stocks in the enclaves, and Dr. Karadzic maintained that the agreement was consistent on removal of Bosnian forces from the demilitarised zone. Are you familiar with this situation?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you comment on Dr. Karadzic noting that UNPROFOR's requirements would be determined by the Bosnian Serb Army headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: This was one of the ways in which the Bosnian Serb authorities modulated/controlled our activities in the eastern enclaves, because not -- it was never just a question of the convoy can pass or it can't pass; it was how big is the convoy, how many trucks, who is on it, what is on it. We had to provide detailed information with every convoy request about the composition of the convoy, and they were able to use that information in two main ways. One was to actually, on an operational level, control what did go and what didn't go in terms of, say, UN weapons, UN communications equipment, fuel, to the enclaves, and they were able, through that, to limit our operational capability in the enclaves. The second way was it gave them a bureaucratic -- a very convenient bureaucratic means by which to block convoys. Your convoy request said there were 13 trucks with these license plates, and you have 13 trucks and 12 of them have the right license plate, 1 has the wrong one, so you have to send the whole convoy back. Or, you know, they would have someone at a check-point somewhere who could find something that wasn't on a manifest. So it was this bureaucratic approach, but not because they wanted to be efficient bureaucrats, but because they wanted to prevent or limit our access to the enclaves. They were able to use this bureaucracy, this ponderous, onerous bureaucracy, that they imposed to prevent our access or limit it, restrict it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On subject of limiting UNPROFOR's operational capacity in the enclaves, perhaps we could go to -- oh, pardon me. Could I have this document as the next Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2454, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To recover my train of thought, perhaps, on the subject of limiting UNPROFOR's operational capacity in the enclaves, we could go to another document, 65 ter 10615. And this jumps forward in time to 11 March 1995, and it's a weekly situation report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you just -- first of all, do you see the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you just, first of all, tell us about these types of documents, the weekly situation reports, how they were generated and what information was typically provided in these documents?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: These weekly reports became a very important document. There were really two people who would draft them, either myself or a colleague, and they ended up, I think, becoming rather influential. They were very sought after. They were widely distributed well beyond the distribution list that's indicated there because they provided the most updated factual information on events that were happening, both political and military, as well as analysis of the senior officials in -- of UNPROFOR in Bosnia. And I don't want to in any way take credit for that, that analysis, but -- I mean, it's signed by someone else, not me, so they deserve the credit for it, but I think the documents were seen as sort of an authoritative statement of both factually what was happening and, more broadly, a sound analysis of events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Based on the sources you alluded to at the beginning of your evidence here today?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, based on all the sources of information available to us; formal reporting from military chain of command in UNPROFOR, the Civil Affairs chain of command. We had Civil Affairs officers dispersed in many parts of the country who were meeting with mayors and displaced persons groups, et cetera, from UN military observers, from our political meetings, from the meetings with member states, from the press, from discussions with aid officials, UN NGO, the full range of information sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in this document, I'd like us to go to page 3, paragraph 7, still on the subject of freedom of movement, paragraph 7 being at the bottom of the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This paragraph 7 states: "Severe restrictions imposed on UNPROFOR by the Bosnian Serbs have limited our ability to deliver supplies to the five enclaves, including Sarajevo; hence, our ability to carry out our mandated responsibilities." And further, the last sentence, I note here that it reads: "The increasingly clear intention of the Bosnian Serb Army appears to be to permit delivery of supplies to the enclaves necessary for our survival, but not those needed in order for us to function." First of all, referring to, as you mention in your statement, the limitation on UNPROFOR's operational capacity in the enclave, is this consistent with what you've just been discussing?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And are you able to comment on this -- what you've described as a clear intention to permit -- on the part of the Bosnian Serb Army to permit only those supplies necessary to the enclaves for your survival?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs had total control over what was transported on a UN convoy, an UNPROFOR convoy, UNHCR convoy. They made the determination. We could propose/request, as we did many, many times. And many, many, many times, our requests were rejected and they only allowed in what they allowed in, and they did not allow in, in many cases, and this is one of those time-periods, they did not allow in many things that we asked for, they did not allow in the supplies that we judged were necessary for us to conduct our mandated operations. The Security Council resolutions made very clear not just what our mandated responsibilities were, but that we were entitled to freedom of movement, full access to the enclaves. The Bosnian Serbs, unfortunately, didn't respect that, and, as a result, we often found ourselves -- our troops in the eastern enclaves did not have the material, the equipment, necessary to conduct their operations. Literally, say, fuel was a good example. They didn't have fuel to conduct patrols. And they -- as suggested in this paragraph, they only wanted to push us so far to allow us to survive, but not function. And by restricting the supplies, dramatically restricting the supplies going in, they were able to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did -- do you know whether this ultimately had an effect on the UNPROFOR forces in the enclaves by the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: It absolutely did have an effect on the UNPROFOR forces, our capabilities in the enclaves; all three, but in particular Srebrenica and Zepa. It had an operational impact, in terms of the material, the equipment, the fuel at the disposal -- the food, fresh rations versus canned rations, et cetera, the communications, the medivac. They oftentimes imposed restrictions on our ability to medically evacuate our personnel. So it had that significant operational impact on our ability, very damaging. It also had a significant psychological impact on our troops there, their commanders, who were so beholden to the Bosnian Serbs for their survival that they started to function in a way where they did not want to do anything that would upset the Bosnian Serbs for fear that more restrictions would be placed on them. They wanted to ingratiate themselves with the Bosnian Serbs so that the Bosnian Serbs might allow food, or mail, or fuel, or whatever in. And meanwhile, because the Bosnian Serbs linked these restrictions at times, the Bosnian Serb authorities, to what they described as inappropriate behaviour by the Bosnian Government or its forces in the enclaves, you know, the fact that there were Bosnian Army soldiers in there, they said basically the message to UNPROFOR, particularly the commanders on the ground, was, You're facing these restrictions because the Bosnian Army, the Bosnian Government, is doing something wrong. Get them to stop it and things will be fine for you. So that put our forces, our commanders on the ground, in the psychological position of being dependent upon the Bosnian Serbs, and wanting to ingratiate themselves with them, and seeing them in some ways as their -- someone who could save them or help them, and saw the Bosnian Government and its forces in the enclaves as the source of their difficult -- the difficult situation in which they were in. It was because of their misbehaviour that they weren't -- it was because of the Bosnian Government forces' misbehaviour that the UNPROFOR forces were not able to eat, or have fuel, or whatever. So it was a very unpleasant situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we leave this document, I'd like us to go from paragraph 7 over to paragraph 9, and it goes back to the subject of Sarajevo. In paragraph 9, you talk about how sniping in the city remained a problem that week, and you discuss a number of incidents. And two-thirds of the way down the paragraph, you note that during a meeting with BH commander General Smith, General Mladic said that: "The increase in sniping by the Bosnian Serb Army in the Sarajevo area was in response to Serb casualties suffered in military offensives launched by the Bosnian Government. (The explicit recollection," in parentheses, "by Mladic of Bosnian Serb Army responsibility for sniping is somewhat surprising)." And you noted in your statement, in regard to this passage, that you recall being struck by this. Now, why is that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I was surprised that General Mladic was admitting something that we all suspected, but that didn't necessarily reflect very well on the Bosnian Serbs; that they were deliberately using sniping to target civilians or to punish the Bosnian Government authorities for actions elsewhere, it was retaliation for something that was happening elsewhere, they were using sniping as a tool, a point of leverage, a way to punish. And we certainly suspected that or saw it that way, but we -- I was surprised to hear General Mladic acknowledge that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this document be a Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. For the record, I note the 65 ter number, which is 10615, and it will be admitted as Exhibit P2455.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to move, actually, on to another topic, and that's the subject of NATO, and in that regard deal with another document you refer to in your written evidence, 65 ter 10608, a report you drafted on 5 December 1994, entitled "Clarification of NATO's Role in Bosnia-Herzegovina," reporting on a meeting between Generals Gvero and Tolimir, on the one hand, and General Rose and Mr. Andreev, on the other hand. Do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to paragraph 4 on page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We see a concern expressed that given misunderstanding by parties to the conflict, the international press, on what NATO's role is in Bosnia, there would be advantages to clarifying this. And then if we go over to the next page of this document, it attaches elements to be included in a statement from New York in this regard, as drafted by General Rose. So on the subject of NATO's involvement in Bosnia and Herzegovina, perhaps you could give us your views, first of all, whether this is consistent, these elements to be included in the statement, consistent with your understanding of NATO's role in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be helpful or would assist us if you could discuss the circumstances or the type of action on the part of either of the factions which would call for NATO's intervention or involvement.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Well, as this document indicates, there are four main areas where NATO would possibly intervene at the request of UNPROFOR. There was the no-fly zone, which, really, because there -- the limited air power capabilities of the parties was not something that was resorting in NATO having to use force. There were some helicopter flights by the parties, but that -- that issue didn't really come up very much. There was the issue of coming to UNPROFOR's assistance, self-defence. And the other three areas: UNPROFOR's self-defence, enforcement of the heavy weapons exclusion zone, and protection of the safe areas. But in order -- in order for NATO to take action, the UNPROFOR had to agree, it had to be at UNPROFOR's request, the request of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General. The threshold, in terms of the level of the violations necessary in order for the SRSG to conclude that the resort to use of force was the appropriate course of action, that threshold was very, very high. It wasn't a formal legal requirement. The legal requirement was rather low, actually. A small violation could have justified, legally, the -- a request by UNPROFOR to NATO to use force. But politically for the United Nations, it was very unpleasant. It was against our nature to call on another party to use military force against someone. We were there as peacekeepers, we wanted to stop the fighting. So in order for us, and this was particularly the case, I think, with the SRSG, to feel that recourse to NATO force was appropriate, it really had to be the last available option. The level of violations had to be so high -- the situation had to be so extreme, the issues at risk, threat to civilian life, et cetera, had to be so present in order for the SRSG to request NATO to use force. There were routine violations of, say, the safe areas or the heavy weapons exclusion zone that could have very easily, from a legal basis, warranted a recourse to force. But if there was just a technical violation, an artillery piece in the heavy weapons exclusion zone that wasn't doing anything, there was no way that UNPROFOR was going to request NATO use of force. It was only when the situation had become quite extreme, civilians were being targeted, heavy weapons within the zone were being used to do the targeting, that UNPROFOR would ask NATO to come to its assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in the case of what you've described as small, or technical, or perhaps, I could ask, single violations, what would UNPROFOR's first line of response have been, then?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: We routinely approached any party that was in violation of its responsibilities, and certainly in the case of these issues, routinely approached the Bosnian Serb authorities, pointing out their violations, whether it was heavy weapons exclusion zone or encroachment by forces towards the safe area, giving them the information, telling them we knew about it, explaining that it was a violation, explaining what our expectations were, what the Security Council mandate required, what their responsibilities were, pointing out what could happen if the violation continued. So we -- 90 -- well, I can't put a specific number on it, but the vast majority of our response to violations was a political one; it was letters, it was meetings, it was dialogue, it was negotiation, it was requests, it was beseeching. It was only in very, very extreme circumstances where we would resort to the use of force.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just before we leave this document, if we could go back to the previous page, please, paragraph 5. I see that General Gvero is recorded as insisting that the opening of the airport was directly connected to the Bosnian Serb Army receiving guarantees that NATO wouldn't strike targets on Bosnian Serb Army territory. Now, we've talked about the airport and the linkage of issues earlier in your testimony, and I wonder, given that, if you have any comment on this.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: This is a good example of the issue that I was describing earlier, where the Bosnian Serb authorities were able to control our use of the airport by providing or withholding the security guarantees necessary for UN flights into the airport, and their willingness at times to link those security guarantees and, hence, the opening or closure of the airport to unrelated issues. The airport was a valuable source of leverage for the Bosnian Serbs, and here they were seeking to use that leverage to obtain something that was extremely important to them, which was the conditions under which NATO would use force, or tried to prevent it entirely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just before we leave the subject of the airport altogether, could you tell us who actually benefitted most from the continued operation of the airport?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: It was a critical -- a critical capability for UNPROFOR to use the airport. That was our point of access into the country, or for the most part. Our leadership used it, our military used it, rotation flights. It was also a critical source of supplies for UNHCR. The air-lift into the city carrying food routinely had 10, 15 more flights a day carrying food for UNHCR. And, of course, the UNHCR flights were bringing humanitarian assistance to the civilian population in Sarajevo, so the population there depended, to a large extent, on the airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this be a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honour, 65 ter 10608?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2456, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to move to another area now, and do this by reference to yet another document you referred to in your written evidence, 65 ter 10709. Now, this document is a weekly BH political assessment, number 81, for the period covering 21 to 27 August 1994, which you drafted. Before we go further into it, could you just explain, briefly, for us what these political assessments were?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: This is the same kind of report as I was referring to earlier. It's the weekly assessment of the main events and political -- I think we later changed it because the assessment went beyond just political issues. So it's basically a summary of the main developments on the ground and an assessment of their meaning for a given week.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we go over to the next page, as I recall, in this document, paragraph 4 -- sorry, page 3, it would be, then. Paragraph 4 reports on something you call a Serb-Serb conflict, and sets out a series of accusations against the Pale leaders by Serbian authorities, including the Serbian prime minister, who accused the Bosnian Serb leadership of committing crimes against humanity, for continuing the war for their own internal reasons, including avoiding the war crimes tribunal, and also President Lilic accused the RS leadership of continued ethnic cleansing and shelling Muslim civilian targets, despite promises to stop. First of all, how would you have become aware of this Serb-Serb conflict and these public accusations?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Well, our -- one of our main responsibilities was to track political developments related to the conflict, and that included all aspects, not just those internal to Bosnia, but relations between the Bosnian Croats and the Croatian Government in Zagreb was something that we paid close attention to. And certainly the relationship between President Milosevic and the authorities in Belgrade, on the one hand, and Dr. Karadzic and the authorities in Pale, on the other, were a very important issue for us because they could have a big impact on the course of the conflict, the political negotiations, et cetera. So it was an issue we paid close attention to. We tried to learn as much about it as we could from a range of sources. One important source of information was, simply, the media, media coming out of Belgrade, for the most part, but also in Bosnia. And I think it's likely that we were aware of these statements by President Lilic and Prime Minister Marjanovic from Belgrade media sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in this -- if we could go over to paragraph 9 in this very same document, we see that despite these public accusations, you reported on ethnic-based expulsions of Muslims from Bijeljina, Banja Luka and Sanski Most the very same week. And at the last line of that paragraph, you note that: "Repeated protests from the UNHCR and ICRC have had no effect on the continuing policy." And I'd like to know on what basis did you consider these expulsions or these incidents to be the manifestations of a policy?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Ethnic-based expulsions started taking place really at the beginning of the conflict. They were an issue that received a lot of international attention. The Security Council resolutions that were passed routinely referred to them and condemned them and demanded that they stop, yet they continued. These were something that the world paid a lot of attention to. There was a lot of pressure on the parties not to engage in this kind of activity, yet it continued. It could not have continued in the case of the ethnic groups that were being expelled or pressured out from the Bosnian Serb-controlled area. It could not have taken place without there being a policy to conduct this. The Bosnian Serb authorities exercised very good control over what happened in their territory. They certainly were able to entirely control, say, our movements on their territory. They could stop a large UNPROFOR convoy with many heavily-armed soldiers and weapons, and they could stop it with a simple check-point. So it's not feasible that large-scale population movements, under pressure sometimes from paramilitary gangs, could take place without the participation, the acquiescence, the role of the Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At the beginning of your evidence today, you talked about the Bosnian Serb war objectives, and you included in that -- and I'll find you the exact reference. You said. "... that they wanted to have or control or define certain territorial space in which they had total political control and in which Bosnian Serbs could live separately from Muslims and Croats ..." And I'm wondering if you see any relationship between these incidents and the war objectives, as you explained them?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: This is the -- these expulsions were the pursuit -- or one of the ways through which those war objectives were pursued. The expulsions also created facts on the ground that would become very hard to reverse through a political process. While the Security Council was condemning ethnically-based expulsions on all sides, the -- and saying that they wouldn't be tolerated and people should be able to return to their homes, I think there was a political reality that once an area was -- was devoid of all ethnic groups except one, it was very unlikely that that particular area would be handed over to a different ethnic group in the course of a political settlement. So by expelling the ethnic groups -- the other ethnic groups from an area, the -- any party, but in this case the Bosnian Serb party by expelling non-Serbs, they were more or less able to assure that they would get the land from which they were expelling people in a peace agreement, even if, in other circumstances, that land may have been contested as part of a peace discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this document, 65 ter 10709, be the next Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2457, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it time for the morning break now, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Quite right. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, we left on a discussion of ethnic cleansing and ethnic-based expulsions of non-Serbs from Banja Luka, Sanski Most and Bijeljina, and I'd like to continue on that subject by moving on to a further document, 65 ter 10658, which is a weekly BiH political assessment for the period covering 4 to 10 September 1994, which you drafted. Do you see it on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could, please, go to page 3 of this document, paragraph 5, that would be helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this paragraph reports the continued expulsion of non-Serbs from Bosnian Serb-controlled territory, in particular from Banja Luka, Sanski Most and Bijeljina. And in paragraph 6, which begins at the very bottom of the page, and if we could go over to the next page, we see that you were present when Mr. de Mello raised this with Dr. Karadzic, in response to which Dr. Karadzic claimed that these people were -- those people departing Banja Luka were doing so of their own volition, whereas those from Bijeljina were forced from their homes by criminal elements akin to Hong Kong mafia. And then he told a press conference, after the meeting, that the Bijeljina expulsions were not the policy of the RS and had been stopped as of 48 hours earlier: "Nonetheless, 1.000 more were expelled that day." First of all, who was Mr. de Mello?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Sergio Vieira de Mello was the head of Civil Affairs for UNPROFOR at that time; based in Zagreb, but with responsibilities for UNPROFOR Civil Affairs as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in regard to this response by Dr. Karadzic, perhaps we could break it down into a couple of parts or three parts. In regard to his assertion that the expulsions were not a policy of the Republika Srpska, do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I think it's clear, from the course of events over the entire war, that ethnic-based expulsions were clearly one of the policies of the Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in regard to his remark to the effect that victims had been forced to leave their homes by criminal elements akin to Hong Kong mafia, you alluded to this earlier in your testimony this morning, and I wonder if you have any comment on this particular remark.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: There were non-state authorities acting in the area controlled by the Bosnian Serbs, paramilitary gangs who were criminal gangs that carried out just atrocious behaviour, atrocities against civilians, non-Serb civilians; plundering, looting, raping, killing, burning, expelling. Such gangs did exist. They operated, though, in my estimation, with full awareness, a connivance, indeed at times support, of the Bosnian Serb authorities. Political -- I mean, everyone knew about the existence of these gangs. Certainly, the political authorities in Pale were aware of them. The degree of co-operation with Bosnian Serb military on the ground, I suppose, varied according to circumstances, according to group, according to time-period, according to geographic area, but there was certainly, at times, co-operation -- active co-operation, in my view. At all times, though, these groups could not have operated without the connivance, the acquiescence, of the Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, finally, Dr. Karadzic observed that these -- at the press conference, Dr. Karadzic observed that these expulsions had stopped 48 hours earlier; nonetheless, a thousand more were expelled that same day. Do you have any observation in regard to Dr. Karadzic's remark?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Well, quite clearly, they -- the expulsions had not stopped if a thousand more were expelled the following day. I think there's also a question with respect to whether people were leaving of their own volition or not, as the paragraph raises. And that concept, I think, very much depends on one's perspective. It may be true, in a certain sense, that in the end, a family or a large number of people decided that they wanted to leave. One needs to, though, consider the circumstances surrounding that decision. And if they -- if neighbours were being tormented, killed, raped, if houses were being burnt, if property was being stolen, if they were being visited at their house by menacing elements, paramilitary elements, saying, Leave or else, and maybe they were offered some free passage out or threatened with some very dire alternative, then, yes, maybe they packed up their bags and left in those cases. Is that of their own volition? In a certain sense, yes, they decided to leave. They, though, perhaps were not given much choice. Clearly, in many cases, people were pressured, through very dire means, to make that decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this document, Your Honour, 65 ter 10658, be marked as a Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2458, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like now to move on to another area, and some months later in the conflict, to document P2258, which is dated 27 March 1995. It was 65 ter 01684, and it should be a report you drafted on a meeting you attended with Mr. Aguilar, General Smith, Professor Koljevic, and Mr. Zametica. Do you recognise -- or do you see the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Aguilar?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Enrique Aguilar was the person who succeeded Victor Andreev as the delegate of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General and the head of Civil Affairs for Bosnia, and he was, in that capacity, my superior after the departure of Mr. Andreev.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this document refers to Mr. Zametica. Who did you understand Mr. Zametica to be?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Jovan Zametica, according to my understanding, was essentially a political advisor to the top Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at the very bottom of page 1 -- of paragraph 1, we see: "Koljevic was stark in his denunciation of Bosnian attacks, and stated ..." If we could go over to page 2. "... that the Serb intention was now to pursue an end to the war through military means." You've alluded to the situation in March and April 1995 earlier in your testimony, and I wonder if you could just, in that regard, put this remark in context for us?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb authorities had objectives that they wanted to accomplish through this war that we discussed earlier, and they had two main avenues available to them to achieve those objectives, military and political. And they, I think, would have preferred to get everything they wanted through political means and not have to pay the price of war, with their own soldiers dying, but their objectives were -- for the most part, their key objectives were not changing or did not change. And when they perceived that they could not achieve their aims through political means, the avenue available to them was a military one. And in March of 1995, at this time when the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement was breaking down, when the peace process was not producing results favourable to them, with what was referred to earlier as the Serb-Serb conflict, they perhaps saw their strategic position weakening, and thought that if they were to achieve their objectives, they were going to have to achieve them through military means, and probably sooner rather than later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we then go over to paragraph 6 of this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You have contextualised this for us, and perhaps I can ask you a question about the very last sentence in paragraph 6. You wrote: "One got the impression from the meeting that Koljevic was serving simply as a messenger, adding further credence to the suggestion that the military is in the ascendancy at the expense of political figures in Pale." What did you mean by this remark?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The conflict, throughout its course, had ebbs and flows. There were periods of time where the political process held out greater promise for all parties that it might bring some resolution of the conflict, and there were times when the political process was manifestly not able to deliver on the parties' war aims. And depending upon the circumstances, the political process was dominant, the military option or the military conflict was dominant. There was always an element of both, but at times, clearly, if, say, the political process was stalled, then the parties were focused on either pursuing their aims through military objectives or at least not losing ground, militarily. In March 1995, at this time, with the political process not delivering results, clearly stalled, then the parties or, in this case, the Bosnian Serb parties, were -- the Bosnian Serb party was looking more toward achieving its aims through military means, which meant the focus was going to be on the Bosnian Serb Army, on how it was going to achieve its objectives, how it was going to advance the objectives of the Bosnian Serbs, and that meant that the military leadership was going to be more dominant than the ones who would otherwise -- say the civilian leaders who would be pursuing a political process. In the absence of a political process, it's natural that the military leaders would be more dominant.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, then, right at around this same time, and I could cite you the paragraph 106 of your statement and a document which I don't need to display, 65 ter 10618, you referred to Karadzic -- Dr. Karadzic appearing in military uniform on 24 March in Lopare, and having seen a video report of that. Given what you've said, do you attribute any significance to Dr. Karadzic's change of garb into military uniform on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I think his -- Dr. Karadzic's appearance in military uniform is fully consistent with exactly what I was just describing, with the focus turning more toward the military. With the focus on the military, that had operational implications, but also psychological ones or morale ones for the Bosnian Serb Army, for the Bosnian Serb people, and Dr. Karadzic's appearance in military uniform, I think, was meant to send a signal to his army, the people, as well as other involved parties, the Bosnian Government, UNPROFOR, other observers, that they were headed down the military path.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To finish off with this discussion, perhaps we could play a short video-clip of about three minutes in length. It's 65 ter 45155. It's in Sanction, so there is a transcript available. And I'm told by Mr. Reid that my colleagues have -- in the booth have been given copies of the transcript as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Today, the president of Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, visited Lopare and Ugljevik, the Podmajevica municipality situated in the immediate vicinity of the combat activity zone which were attacked in the most recent Muslim offensive on Majevica. While talking with people, leadership and military commanders, Mr. Karadzic indicated the seriousness of the situation and our determination to endure in these critical moments. In addition to the analysis of the military situation, the actual situation at the battlefield, the economic, political and executive power, and the life in the combat environment were also discussed. "Dear viewers, here, at the height of the Muslim offensive on the Majevica, the president our republic is in Lopari, socialising with the population and the people of the area. Mr. President, what are your first impressions?" "The impressions are that these people are cheerful and spirited, and that they know what they want, and that they are adamant to defend their country. It is the same in the army, the morale is excellent. Equipment and the decisiveness bear no objection or reproach. On the contrary, there has been a total, well-founded optimism, and I think we could do something similar as we did when they attacked us from Bihac. That is to say that, for us, Tuzla is no more a protected zone. It is a stronghold and a headquarters of the 2nd Corps of the Muslim Army wherefrom they advanced towards our territories to endanger the Serbian Majevica, to endanger the relay, which, by the way, did not fall. Therefore, the people need to know that. I believe that we now have all the legitimate rights to return and to pursue the enemy up to, and if it need to be so, Tuzla also." "You are rarely in uniform. Hence, each uniform on you is a warning that something serious is going on." "Well, no, it's not that they are forcing us to put uniforms on. If we put on uniforms, the whole of the nation will be putting them on, if necessary. We are fighting up to a measure, a minimum one, to which we consider it necessary to protect our interests. However, if they force all of us to really put uniforms on and centralise the procurement, even to proclaim a state of war, then there will be no cease-fire and we'll go for the total destruction of our enemies. So far, we wanted to enable this war to end in a draw. They obviously do not want it, and it is our commitment now, our orientation, that the enemy must be destroyed on the Majevica area first and foremost, and then further on towards our territories. Finally, Tuzla also used to be ours, and there is no reason for us to give it up." "Since the whole world knows that it is the case, that it is about a big offensive of the Muslim side, what did you, as supreme commander, warn our commanders of?"
