"Well, certain orders have been issued, and I was pleased to notice yesterday, during the day, that they had been elaborated and descended up to the corps command and further down there. Our army knows precisely what they should do. The enemy who approached our positions and tried breakthroughs should be destroyed, and we will not stop at it. We have a legitimate right to a counter-offensive. The very important thing is that the whole world has seen who broke the cessation of hostilities. I would like to say to our viewers that the truce and the cessation of hostilities considerably differ. A truce is being violated, but a cessation of hostilities is an act that straightaway proceeds to the signing of a total peace, that is to say, the end of the war. Even that was not sacrosanct to the Muslims. They were using this truce, cessation of hostilities to arm themselves, and at the moment when they estimated that it did not suit them anymore, they breached it prudently. The whole of the international community sees it, and now we can do whatever we want and we will be pursuing them and destroying them."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, the time code for this clip has stopped at 3:47.4.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, is this the video-clip you reported on?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Having heard now the English translation of the interview of Dr. Karadzic, and -- having heard the English translation, do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I noticed he referred -- Dr. Karadzic referred, early in the clip, to the morale of the civilian population, as well as that of the military, and I see that consistent with my earlier comments about the purpose of Dr. Karadzic appearing in uniform. It was, in part, to bolster the morale of the military and the civilian population, show leadership at a difficult time, indicate that they are headed down a certain course, and his comments about the conflict and how the Bosnian Government or Bosnian Muslims, as was said, had decided on a course of war; that the Bosnian Serbs were now going to defeat their enemy. So it's all very consistent, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You referred earlier in your testimony to Dr. Karadzic as a supreme commander, a man who straddled the political and military spheres. Is this also consistent with your assessment in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, and I think there were some comments in the clip that indicated as much in terms of his -- he was referred to, I believe, in the clip by the reporter as supreme commander, and then he made reference to reviewing orders that had been passed down. So, yes, I think it is also consistent.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could this be the next Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2459, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, that concludes my examination-in-chief, and I would like now to move into evidence all those associated exhibits which have not otherwise been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In your list, there are certain exhibits that have already been admitted, such as Exhibit 2258, which we dealt with just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think my colleague, the Registrar, has identified three additional, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Three additional. I noted two additional, so let's find out. The first one is 10616, which has been admitted as P2257, and 10652, which has been admitted as Exhibit D1034. Do you have anything further?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't, Your Honour. I was relying on my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And during your examination-in-chief, we admitted 09686, 10608, 10615, 10628, 10658, 10709, and 11172.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this last video, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which was not part of associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And my last question: In relation to 11192 and 11193, do we have them in our e-court? I don't think they are, they haven't been up-loaded yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for just a brief moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see, no, they have not. And, indeed, they will be forthwith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any objections from the Defence, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then those that haven't been admitted will be admitted and given a number by the Deputy. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Mr. Karadzic, are you ready to start your cross-examination? Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning to all. Welcome back, Excellency, welcome back to our midst.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Banbury. First of all, I would like to thank you for having been so kind as to meet up with the Defence as well. Yesterday, we conducted an interview, and I hope that that will make it possible for us to go through your testimony faster and in an easier way. First of all, I would like to ask you something briefly. Let us recall the documents that you wrote for your -- or, rather, drafted for your superiors. Am I right if I say that, as much as possible, without stenographic notes, you wrote down what it was that happened during the course of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The end of the document usually contains certain assessments from the political and military aspects; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who actually made these assessments?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: In the documents that I drafted, I was the one who would prepare the assessments. It depended. Sometimes, say, if there was a meeting in Pale, and on the drive back to Sarajevo there may have been a discussion in the vehicle on the significance of the meeting, and I would take away some conclusions from that discussion with, say, my superior, and thus incorporate his thoughts into the assessment. At other times, I simply did it entirely on my own. My superior, who ultimately signed the document, of course, had the ability to change the assessment, to change elements of it, but normally the assessment that I initially drafted was left largely, if not entirely, untouched.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in the first part, although there were no stenographic notes that were taken, were all the most important things that were said during the course of meetings actually written up?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, that was the -- my main or one of my main aims, to ensure that the report accurately reflected the facts of the meeting, the main points, the main discussion, in an objective way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So could we then say that the first part of a document was the most objective one, and that the conclusion at the end was somewhat less objective?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution expected you -- expected to introduce many documents drafted or written by you, and to introduce them through you. That will help both the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber, but that gives me a task to differentiate between facts and opinions, impressions and so on. Would you agree that your comments, because we have the first part of the document, which is the most objective one, then the assessment at the end, which is somewhat less objective, would you agree that your comments are even less objective; that by the very nature of things, they have to be subjective?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that we should always differentiate between what you knew for certain, and mentioned as a fact, and what was your assessment, or opinion, or impression, or belief?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise the important distinction between facts and assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to say that you were always very correct when you said -- when something that you stated was an impression, so this will make our work easier. And now, Mr. Banbury, I would like to focus on a subject, the subject of ethnic cleansing. The following paragraphs of your statement refer to it: 48 and 49, and then 60 through 63, and 87 through 89. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Before that, I wonder if you have your statement before you, Mr. Banbury.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's great, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not comment on specific paragraphs, but just so we know what is located where, in case we need it. I would now ask for document 65 ter 1294. If we could please see that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree, Mr. Banbury, that the summer and fall of 1994 were marked by the work of the Contact Group? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please have a look at this document, dated the 9th of September, 1994, in which HCA Vieira de Mello travelled to Pale, where he held talks with the leadership of Republika Srpska. Can you please have a look at this document a bit, the first page, and then we'll move on to the second page. Could we now please show the second page on the screen. Due to a large number of documents, we have to skip the issues that I'm not primarily interested in. But the document is available to everyone. Can you please pay attention to paragraph 5: [In English] "... HCA then called for the early re-opening the airport routes, noting that their closure was raising concern over the strangulation of Sarajevo and imposing hardship on the civilian population ..." [Interpretation] And so on. Do you remember that you said today that I stated that the reason for closing the airport was my wish to demonstrate who had control over the airport?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I remember reference to that quote on VOA, that -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that we handed over the airport to the United Nations so that they can use it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I was not in Bosnia when the control of the airport was taken by UNPROFOR. It's my understanding that there was a conflict over the airport and UNPROFOR was able to take control, in part, because of decisions made by the Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, we'll show the agreement and we did hand it over. But please have a look at paragraph 6 now. It refers to ethnic cleansing, and it says here: [In English] "HCA then appealed to Karadzic to put an end to the ethnic cleansing in Banja Luka and Bijeljina, and to make public his intention to seize the criminal network, in accordance with assurances given three weeks earlier to Akashi and himself. Karadzic confirmed, both privately and in the public statements subsequently issued to the press, that such practices did not reflect his policies, were damaging to the Serb cause, that Bijeljina's police chief had been replaced, and that two small independent gangs had been identified." [Interpretation] Is that what you testified about today, and can you see from this that certain names are mentioned of people who were working with Muslims, making lists, or imposed tolls on them? Did you know all this?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't exactly understand the question. What are you asking of me? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that we informed you, privately and through the press, that we had replaced the police chief, not because he had done something, but because he was not successful in preventing this from happening? And you can see further down in paragraph 6 that this name is mentioned, a person who may be acting under somebody else's instructions, and that this was our position.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: That was -- I confirm that was the stated position that you passed on to Mr. de Mello in that meeting. That's what you said. That accurately reflects what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at something that's at the end of paragraph 7, where it says that I agreed to allow local political leaders, the Muslim political leaders, to travel to Sarajevo to meet personally with Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1136, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today, during examination-in-chief, you agreed -- or, rather, stated that the problem of ethnic cleansing was present on all sides from the very beginning; correct? That is to say, that it did not arise in September or during the summer of 1994, but that it was a problem that lasted much longer than that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: It's correct that the problem took -- was a problem throughout the conflict and that there were population movements on all sides, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also said that the Security Council condemned all sides, but then, in continuation, you said, We would then warn the Serbian side. Would you agree that the Security Council condemned all three sides for such practices, but that you condemned and warned just the Serbian side? I don't mean you, personally, but the UN.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The Security Council made very clear, through their resolutions as well as presidential statements, that they condemned the practice of ethnic cleansing, no matter who was responsible. And UNPROFOR, its leadership, would, as a matter of policy and practice, condemn any instances of ethnic cleansing over which they became aware and raise it with authorities -- the senior authorities of the party responsible. So I think it's really the case that when and if other parties to the conflict were responsible for ethnic cleansing, UNPROFOR raised it with them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see 1D0245 [as interpreted]. It is a document that was issued on the eve of your arrival, but it refers to the same subject. You arrived on the 9th or 10th of April. The date of this document is the 2nd of April, but it talks about an ongoing problem; right? Could we please see 1D02455.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, Mr. Karadzic: Mr. Banbury, and this is para 6 of this document, Mr. Karadzic seemed to have been referring to Arkan's gangs or something like that, which you refer to as elements akin to Hong Kong mafia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe the term "Hong Kong mafia" was my term. I believe it was Dr. Karadzic's term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you stated that there were non-state authorities acting in the area controlled by the Bosnian Serbs, paramilitary gangs, who were criminal gangs that carried out just atrocities. What was your basis to state -- to conclude in such a way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were -- I think it was well established that there were paramilitary gangs, led by notorious figures, some from Bosnia, some from Serbia proper, that carried out a range of unpleasant activities in Bosnia. They were more dominant in the early stages of the war than in the latter stages, but I think their existence was not disputed. It was -- they were widely reported on through the press, through UN reporting, complaints -- we received complaints about them from Bosnian Government authorities or Croatian authorities. There was witness testimony, victim testimony, about the activities of these gangs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My mistake. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a letter from Prime Minister Dr. Vladimir Lukic. You can see who this is addressed to. And now please have a look at the first paragraph: [In English] "We have received UNHCR report on the deteriorating situation in Banja Luka. It is rather interesting that this is in the first report of the minority status anywhere in the former B and H, and even more interesting that UNHCR produced it to attract the attention of the international community and the media. Unfortunately, it leaves us in no doubt that the UN agency is becoming involved in the war against the Serbs." [Interpretation] And a bit down, a bit down: [In English] "... UNHCR officials, it seems, do not check the sources of the collected information, nor its contents, and uncritically use statements of Bishop, Mufti, and Caritas representatives in the field. They request the protection of the minorities, but they do not seem to be interested in a number of criminal charges brought in the region against individuals engaged in criminal activities of damaging the property of Muslims or Croats." [Interpretation] Were you aware that we arrested and prosecuted elements who conducted themselves unlawfully towards the Muslims and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I am not aware of the prosecutions -- arrests or prosecutions that the Bosnian Serb authorities may have conducted against criminal elements of this nature. No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is this consistent with what I was saying about this in September, before you, concerning the situation in Banja Luka and the same topic?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Well, the -- your statements are consistent on this, in terms of what you've just said, but the -- according to what I know or what I am aware of, the main perpetrators of these acts, the leaders of these gangs, they were not arrested or prosecuted. They were able to act with impunity and carry on their activities over the course of a long period of time. So the statements may be consistent. What I'm aware of, in terms of what happened on the ground, is slightly different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You will be surprised, if you follow this trial to the end, to know how many people we put behind bars. Can we please see the following page. The prime minister, Mr. Lukic, observes here that Louis Gentille and the others -- actually, that there were 29 municipalities in the Banja Luka region, and that whatever was going on in these remote and poorly controlled municipalities was ascribed to Banja Luka, as if the entire region was the town of Banja Luka, itself. And you can see here, in the first paragraph, what social and refugee status the population in the region had: [In English] "It is absurd to raise the problem of jobs because of -- the largest number of the population lost them, thanks to the care of the international community to implement vigorous sanctions against the Serbs." [Interpretation] Therefore, it was the sanctions which caused people to be dismissed. Then there was a huge number of refugees who came to that region, and there were objections that the Croats and Muslims were not being employed, which later on produced something that you noticed. It was a reason for them to request to leave. Please have a look at the second paragraph now, which says: [In English] "... especially that not even a word has been said on the situation of the Serbs in Sarajevo. We know that by now some 7.000 Serbs have been liquidated by Muslim militias in Sarajevo. Not a single Serb is allowed to leave Sarajevo without the permission of Muslim authorities ..." [Interpretation] And somewhat lower down, the last paragraph: [In English] "... political involvement of international humanitarian agencies may have foreseen consequences, and it represents a direct interference in the negotiating process that should bring political solution to the former B and H and Yugoslavia." [Interpretation] In the midst of negotiations about the Contact Group plan, a secret Muslim organisation in Banja Luka was preparing an uprising and launched information, and the UNHCR then accepted this and obstructed the implementation of the Contact Group plan. Were you aware of the existence of this Muslim organisation in Banja Luka at the time which was doing all this?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: No, I'm unaware of that group or activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We will prove this over time. And do you remember that always during conferences or important meetings, there were deteriorations which were aimed at obstructing or at least influencing the particular conference or the development that was happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I believe it was often the case that different parties to the conflict, in advance of an important meeting or conference, would try to influence the situation to their advantage in using different means, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think there's enough there, Your Honour. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1137, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 1D2737, please. On the following day, you will see what my reaction was, and it was distributed to all organs that it had to do with. We also have the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this document and read where I say I order -- it says here I order to all the authorities and all check-points that this can refer to, and I especially emphasise the need to shed light on the crimes committed in Prijedor. You can see the points there. Let me not read it all out. Everyone can see that: "Take all the necessary measures. Remove all administrative obstacles. Provide a police escort for International Red Cross convoys. All our authorities are obliged to ensure complete safety for the International Red Cross personnel." And: "The failure to carry out this order or its incomplete execution will entail the strictest consequences." Mr. Banbury, is this consistent with what I told you and your associates during these negotiations and meetings?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The document here is consistent with your statement that was referred to in the previous code cable.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1138, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may. In regard to this document, I just note, actually, two different signature blocks. It suggests to me that they aren't necessarily translations of one another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- but an English and Srpski version of this same document written for consumption of a wide audience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that the English version was the original one, copied to ICRC at that time. Do you like both of them admitted as separate exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm just trying to figure out a good way to track them, and I'm just not sure if that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that's reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At least, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit it as Exhibit D1138. Yes, leave them as they are, yeah. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see 1D3477. I hope that this is the only document of the 150 or 200 which has not been translated, but it only shows how this order of mine was implemented at the level of the army. This is a telegram from the Ministry of Defence. It says on top -- if you can please show the top, it says "The Ministry of Defence, Banja Luka." If we can see the fax line, please. The Ministry of Defence. It's the 3rd of April, and the telegram sent in the usual code, urgently encoded. The same document is distributed. It's verbatim. So my previous order was now turned into their order and distributed in the army. Item 1: "Take all investigative measures to shed light on crimes, especially in Prijedor." Item 2: "Take all other measures." Number 3: "Remove all administrative obstacles." And so on and so forth. Everything is exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So would you agree that this was prompt action on the part of the Ministry of Defence because this was distributed on the very same day?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I don't speak Serbo-Croat, so I don't know the contents of the document. But assuming it's as you described, then, yes, I would certainly agree it's prompt action.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have this admitted as MFI until such time when we have the translation ready?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There's a CLSS translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excellent. Yes, that will be Exhibit D1139.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see D705. It has been admitted, so just to have a look at it briefly. To show the document to the witness, actually. D705, please. We are still in the month of April, and we are dealing with similar issues. Mr. Akashi sends this telegram to Annan and Stoltenberg on the 7th of April. Can we please have a look at page 3 of this document. Paragraph 10, let us please focus on that: [In English] "In response to my request that the ICRC be allowed to evacuate Muslims from Prijedor, Dr. Karadzic said that the situation in Prijedor was an unfortunate development for the Serbs. While he accepted that the situation could have been predicted (he noted that civilians in the town had, at the beginning of the war, slaughtered each other), he maintained that the present situation had been prompted by a Muslim massacre of six Serb policemen from the town. Currently, additional forces have been sent to the town to stabilise the situation, and he had initially agreed to the ICRC request to evacuate individuals who feared for their lives, based on the belief that the numbers concerned were minimum. However ..." [Interpretation] Could we move to the next page, please, and this continuation you can read: [In English] "However, the ICRC then indicated that they intended to evacuate 80 truckloads of people at one go, and this was unacceptable. He had," means Radovan Karadzic, "he had no objection to them evacuating up to five trucks of people a day (approximately 100 people), as this would allow those left behind to reconsider their situation in light of the stabilised conditions in the town." [Interpretation] And can you please look at this paragraph 12, which speaks about ethnic cleansing and the violation of human rights, and that it would need to stop and so on and so forth. And then Karadzic says: "... that he would welcome my visit to Banja Luka and proposed that the deputy prime minister of the interior, based in Banja Luka, be the host of my trip. If possible, and if he were available, he would also accompany me on my visit." [Interpretation] The last sentence: [In English] "He further noted that the extremists in Banja Luka were difficult to control, and he hoped that my visit would discourage them from future abuses in the area."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you were also aware that a large number of Serbs from Cazinska Krajina had fled to Banja Luka, also from Central Bosnia, and there had to have been people among them who were not familiar to the local police?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This document is already admitted. I just wanted to show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this also comport with your experiences about what I was saying at meetings that you already attended or were already there for?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I think the date of that cable was April 7th, 1994. And I was deployed on April 9th, so this -- these discussions were happening just as I was arriving, so it's hard for me to -- you know, I don't have personal experience of that meeting or I didn't prepare that code cable. I'm reading it, and I -- I think it's an UNPROFOR document, and I think it reflects what was discussed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have D471. It's also a document that's been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, Mr. Banbury, I'm going to tell you about our position on the events, especially those relating to the conferences. It is our assertion that it was not only the local population that was afraid, but also the central Muslim leadership issued instructions to create certain crises and to have the population move out, especially coinciding with certain conferences. Does this sound familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I'm unaware of that practice on the part of the Bosnian Government authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you just please look at this document, then. We also have a translation. This is the SDA, Party of Democratic Action, the main Muslim party, and the document states in the first paragraph: "As the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the security point of view, is becoming more and more complex, especially after the acceptance of the Geneva documents by Karadzic and his clique in Pale, it is necessary, for the purpose of realising the aspiration of all Muslims, the preservation and strengthening of our state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to undertake urgently the following measures in the Trebinje municipality:" And then the demands are listed here: to leave the municipality, as a group, in an organised manner in order to create a crisis; and the SDA also says that they were supposed to report in Montenegro to the Merhamet and the Liberal Association of Montenegro. This is an authentic document of the SDA party, creating a crisis in Trebinje. Do you know that there were no killings in Trebinje, for the most part - this is the 20th of January, 1993 - and that we were proud of the fact that Trebinje managed to preserve its multi-ethnic character?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: If the question is was I aware that there were no killings of Bosnian Muslims in Trebinje in January 1993, I don't know the history well enough. I'm not familiar with the particular circumstances in Trebinje at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that we would inform you at meetings that Muslims were creating certain incidents and making moves that were making the situation more difficult? Do you recall that we did mention Muslim tricks and that you often wrote that down in your notes and reports?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that, on multiple occasions, the Bosnian Serb authorities informed the UNPROFOR leadership that the Bosnian Government or Bosnian Muslims were conducting tricks, so to speak, in order to deceive UNPROFOR, the international community. And we did take note of your warnings in that regard, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D3439, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That document shouldn't be displayed, and it should be used only in private session if it's going to be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just look at the last page, please. And if necessary, we need to go into private session. It's not even necessary to see to whom I said it. We just need to see what I said and what is reported in the document. The parties can look at the document. Can we look at the last part -- the page of the document, and the parties need not see which document it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you look at paragraph 30, please: [In English] "Karadzic said there was no --"

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If Dr. Karadzic is going to quote from the document, we should be doing this in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought perhaps just the last sentence that relates to Trebinje, without referencing the occasion, when I said it and to whom I said it. But if it has to be in private session, then, all right. But let's look at the last sentence of paragraph 30. Can we all look at that, and really that does not reveal anything to anybody, and it can be put in the transcript as confirmation of what I am saying. May I read the last sentence. [In English] "... referring to his letter --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if you are going to refer to a specific passage in this document, we go into private session. Let's do that. We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That document's not being broadcast, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, do you agree that these words of mine reiterate that we had always been proud of the multi-ethnic character of Trebinje? And do you agree that we warned about this pattern of trickery, war trickery, during the war, particularly, let's say, in light of the document that we showed earlier?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I agree that the document you showed earlier included a reference to your statement of pride of the multi-ethnic character of Trebinje, and I agree that you and other senior officials of the Bosnian Serb authority did warn UNPROFOR on -- at times that the Muslim authorities or the Bosnian Government was conducting tricks or attempts to deceive UNPROFOR about various issues, including with respect to reasons for ethnic cleansing or sources of attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like us to shed a little bit of light on this. At the point in time when this was told to me, without having the document of the SDA, would you agree that I did not deny or reject the possibility that that was so, and that I had promised that I would do something about it? And would you recall that on several occasions, I did accept the possibility, and that we would do something about it without accepting that it was really so?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: The document referred to earlier refers to events in January 1993, which is about 15 months before my arrival, and I did not have time to really read the document. So I can, again, agree that the document referred to your statement expressing pride for the multi-ethnic character of Trebinje, and I again acknowledge or agree that you, as well as other senior officials of the Bosnian Serb authorities, on multiple occasions told UNPROFOR -- warned UNPROFOR that the Bosnian authorities were attempting to deceive us in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember the crisis about Banja Luka and Bijeljina, and also the fact that I didn't deny that it happened until I found out what exactly happened? Would you agree that our approach was not to deny anything, but to say, All right, we're going to carry out an investigation to see what happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I -- having read the previous couple documents, I agree that those documents say that. I was not personally involved in those events or those meetings, or those documents -- the preparation of those documents, so it's -- I agree, but only based on the display of the documents here and me reading passages from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you allow for the possibility -- we saw at the meeting of the 9th of September, 1994. Do you accept or do you allow for the possibility that similar instructions were issued to Muslims in Banja Luka and Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were or they weren't. It's, in theory, possible. I wouldn't necessarily know if it had happened. I'm unaware.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'm going to show a document that served as the basis for regular permissions for the population to relocate. This is a document from 1992. Can we look at 1D251 now, please. Can we admit the previous document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1140, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under seal, isn't it? Can we look at 1D251 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The previous document being the one that the witness wasn't asked any related question on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think, yes. So you are objecting to the admission of that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't think the witness was asked a single question related to that document whatsoever. The question was about something to do with Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may respond. I asked about the pattern, and the witness confirmed that we did warn about the pattern. And the document explains the previous document by the Party of Democratic Action, so there's a double connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the context, we find the document to be relevant. On that basis, we admit it. Let us move on. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, you, yourself, said during our interview that you were mostly informing yourself about documents that were drafted before your time and that served as the basis for the presence of the United Nations in Bosnia, particularly documents such as agreements whose duration was not -- was unlimited. This is a document that talks about the treatment towards citizens who wanted to change their place of residence. This is an agreement that was signed by the parties, by representatives of all the parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina, even those from Croatia. Actually, no, it was from the Croatian Democratic Union, and this is a document from the 30th of October, 1992. If necessary, we can look at the Serbian version also. And can we please move to page 2 of this document. This is something that was created at the prompting of the International Red Cross. We're looking at paragraph 3 now: [In English] "... recalling that the presence of civilians may be used to render certain areas immune from military operations." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. This is all the preamble. And now item 1: [In English] "Civilians who desire to leave temporarily the territory controlled by one party to reach the territory controlled by another party should be entitled to do so." [Interpretation] We can skip 2. Everybody can look at that for themselves. And then paragraph 3: [In English] "The civilians should be able to leave in an organised transfer under international supervision and, if necessary, protection. Its security will be guaranteed by each party on the territory it controls." [Interpretation] Item 4: [In English] "Each party to the conflict guarantees to those who leave temporarily the territory it controls: "A) that their goods, assets and belongings will be respected and protected; "B) that they have a right to return home at a later stage if they wish so." [Interpretation] And can we have the last page so that we can look at the signatures. And we can also look at the last paragraph. It's not necessary to read it. It states here that that is a vulnerable group and they would have international assistance, including the ICRC. And then we have four parties that are signatories here. This is not a document of the United Nations, but does this document of the ICRC shed some light on certain transfers?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: This document, again, was written well before my arrival, October 1992. It's my understanding that the provisions contained in the document for the terms of transfers were not regularly respected and they do not characterise the nature of population movements in Bosnia during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I were to tell you, Mr. Banbury, that it was only the Serbian side that provided escorts to civilians who wanted to temporarily relocate, and that the Muslim side expelled Serbs with only a bundle in their hands and with shots, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: There are two parts to that. On the issue of provision of security for Muslims who were departing Bosnian Serb-controlled area, yes, I'm aware that was the -- at times, the case, often the case. I believe that is, in large part, because the departure of those civilians was an objective that was pursued by the Bosnian Serb authorities, and the Bosnian Serb authorities wanted those people to leave, so they escorted them out. I'm unaware of, for instance, any time where private interviews by an impartial international body were conducted to determine the voluntary nature of those departures. In terms of the second part of the conditions under which Serbs departed Bosnian Government-controlled area, I think those -- there were so many instances of that, and the conditions varied from -- according to circumstances. And I know that there were very unpleasant conditions under which Serbs were forced or pressured to depart Bosnian Government-controlled area, and I'm also aware that there were very regularised departure of Bosnian Serbs from government-controlled areas. So I think the circumstances varied quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last question before the break, and I must note here, Mr. Banbury - I believe, that is - after confirming what you knew, you expressed your belief, and this is what is presenting problems to the Defence and something that we must test. Did you have evidence of that or was that a belief? Can you please look at what I said in the previous document. It was D705, in relation to Prijedor: [In English] "He had no objections to them evacuating up to five trucks of people a day, as this would allow those left behind to reconsider their situation in light of the stabilised conditions in the town." [Interpretation] It was not the state policy for them to leave, but for the situation to stabilise and to stop the reasons why they wished to leave in the first place. And does this paragraph 10 confirm that without any doubt, without any "I believe," just about what it is that we know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it would be very difficult, not only for the witness but for the Bench as well, to follow without seeing the document. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this document? And then we can just confirm it, call it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, we are at -- I take it he is talking about 1D251 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the document. Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's deal with it at the end. So why don't we put your question in relation to this document, which is D705.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the following page, please, paragraph 10. It begins here with this page. Here, we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is Mr. Akashi's report concerning his meeting with Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So regardless of the belief, what is expressed here is our attempt not to evacuate 80 trucks, but 5 trucks, even though we were forced to do that as well. We were opposed to that. You will see later that we objected to that, but the reason was for the rest to have time to review their situation so that they would stay in town. Does this document not say that, explicitly?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: This document says that, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, can we take the break now, if that is your decision, and can we admit the previous document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, what about 1D251?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I got a little bit confused between which document we were referring to, and I thought this was all about D705. Could I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, 1D251, ICRC document. I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I answer you after the break, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at five past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I have to address you in relation to the time allocated for this witness. The Prosecution, understandably, had the ambition to have this witness authenticate the documents that he authored. However, in addition to the subjective assessments at the end of these documents, in this statement he provided an enormous number of his interpretations based on impressions, beliefs, certain psychological characteristics as well. So each and every one of these words, if it is treated as evidence, requires the Defence to shed more light on that or, rather, to illuminate it and see that even some other UN documents contest what he says. If the number of words for the final brief and final arguments were not limited, we could deal with it that way. However, believe me, within six hours we cannot indicate everything that is erroneous and unacceptable as a personal interpretation of the man who was actually writing all of that down, who was not an expert, who presents his own views. These are minor alterations. You will see today, when we go on working, for example, he says that Mladic acknowledged to have fired at civilians, although he did not acknowledge that. He acknowledged that there were snipers there who were legitimate, that is, legal. So there are minor matters like that that have mega consequences, as it were. So the Trial Chamber will either neglect his comments or I should be given time to illuminate all of this with him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, six hours is still a long time, a sufficient time to cover important matters. I'll give you an example that you are not spending your time efficiently. We admitted Exhibit D1139, which was prompted -- which is a Ministry of Defence order which was prompted by your order, which was Exhibit D1138. There was no need for you to show the -- this first document to the witness, which could be admitted as a bar table motion or which could be tendered through another witness. That's a minor example. But at this moment, the Chamber is not minded to give you an extension of the time allotted for this witness, so please concentrate on the efficient use of your time. Ms. Edgerton, shall we discuss the admission of the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted. In the meantime, let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1141, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just recall that there are 214 paragraphs, and each and every one of them requires further illumination, and that really puts a great deal of difficulties before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the previous document has been admitted; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3459.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, I would like to put this to you, the continuity of the documents that regulate the treatment of civilians, the continuity of documents that were worked on. The previous one was done with the Red Cross, and this one with the co-chairman of the conference, those who took over from Lord Carrington, the Conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 27th of August, 1992. I would like to draw your attention to these paragraphs that have been marked, where it says how civilians should be treated; that they should not be detained in any way. Look at D, repatriation to areas under the control of their respective ethnic authorities. Can we have the next page, please. Choosing to stay temporarily in the area of detention; relocation in areas away from the conflict under international supervision; and temporary refuge in third countries. Can we go down a bit, can we scroll down? And look at 3.3. It reiterates: "That refugees and displaced persons should be allowed to return voluntarily and safely to their places of origin." Can we have the next page, please. Let's look at number 7: [In English] "That all such actions should be in accordance with the agreement with the parties reached in Geneva on 22nd May under the auspices of the ICRC." [Interpretation] So already at the beginning of the war, one month into the war, the sides signed an agreement, stating how the civilians will be treated, referring to their right to temporarily cross to another territory. I believe that we're going to find that document, too, of the 22nd. And please have a look at B: [In English] "That no party can be expected to give guarantees of security on behalf of the other parties to the conflict." [Interpretation] Do you remember, Mr. Banbury, that both the Muslim and the Serb sides were so close, in terms of the lines in Sarajevo, that both could fire at aircraft?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So much for guarantees. Do you agree that one should take into account all of these agreements, in terms of the temporary relocation of the population, at their own request and in an organised way?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that one should bear in mind all of these agreements that are a basis for the treatment of civilians in this civil war?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I do absolutely agree that all the signed commitments should be taken into account, and I believe UNPROFOR did take them into account. One of our great frustrations was that on many occasions, commitments entered into in the course of political discussions were not respected in practice. So I think it is important to differentiate between commitments that were undertaken by -- voluntarily undertaken by the parties, commitments that were imposed upon them through international humanitarian law, the Security Council resolutions, and the practice of the parties, and there were differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that from the point of view of criminal law, it should be established beyond any doubt whether someone was forced to leave or whether someone had asked to relocate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is not for the witness to answer that question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One has to look rather hard to find a link between the document and the question put to the witness, actually, Your Honour. But certainly it's an authentic document, and on that basis I wouldn't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm still wondering whether or not you had to present -- show this document to the witness in order to put that question, but we'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, the Muslim side managed to convince you that they were in favour of a multi-ethnic Bosnia-Herzegovina; right? And to this day, you remain so convinced, and you speak of that in paragraph 204 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I believed at the time and I believe now that it was the official policy and goal of the Bosnian Government to have a multi-ethnic state, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what I would like to put to you: that at secret meetings with the representatives of Croatia, the Muslim side said that they wanted to expel Serbs from Bosnia, and that the Croats informed the Americans about that. And now I'm going to show another document to you where Ganic says this to President Tudjman. 127, 1D127, can I have that, please? Thank you. Please take a look. This is a record of a meeting, or a transcript of a meeting, between President Tudjman and Ejub Ganic. Please look at page 23 now. In English, it is page 4 in e-court. This is what Ganic is saying: "Mr. President, maybe I'm unrealistic, but I think that the strengthening of the Federation would marginalise the Serbian entity, in particular, if you understand what I'm saying." Can we have the next page? In English, it is still page 4. This last paragraph down here, Ganic is saying: "You know what the world will allow us to do. We can marginalise the Serbs in Bosnia." Can we have page 29? In English, it is page 4. We still have page 4 in English. "Another thing, allow us to arm more, to agree to allow us to receive more weapons. We have a population that is ready for war. What do you think about that? Do you believe Americans or Germans ..." Et cetera. And, Mr. Banbury, that is happening on the 29th of April, 1995. The translation is as I had put it, that we would push into war. That is what the original actually says, and that is as I had said it, we would push a generation into war. So, Mr. Banbury, is this in line with our suspicions regarding the intentions of the Muslims vis-a-vis the Serbs? We told you, the UN, about that as well. The Muslims wanted to have a Bosnia without Christians; first of all, without any Serbs, and then without any Croats either. And see here, this is proof of that. To marginalise the Serbs has become a state project, because this man is the vice-president of the Muslim Presidency and he is the number-one man for running the army of the Bosnian entity.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Dr. Karadzic. Was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of this? Was it not the case that we kept telling you about our fears in relation to the intentions of the Muslims? Does this fit with our trepidation as to what was awaiting us?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Before I answer, could I just ask for a clarification? What was the date of this meeting, please? I didn't notice it when you put on the cover page. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 29th of April, 1995. We can go back to the first page so that you can see.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. The statement by Mr. Ganic quoted in the document, that it was their intention to marginalise the Serbs, I don't know what he meant by "marginalise." That term can mean many different things. But it was certainly the case that there was a federation signed between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats and that that two-party federation was, de facto, aligned against the Bosnian Serbs. And certainly you and other Bosnian Serb leaders did provide UNPROFOR officials with various kinds of warnings or statements that the Bosnian Government, the Bosnian Muslims, wanted to dominate the Serbs, or mistreat the Serbs, or do other things along those lines, so you did provide that -- those kinds of warnings at times, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, or, rather, the parts that I have read out, or all of it, perhaps, the entire document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is actually a document in its original language of more than 40 pages. As far as I understand these materials, just from having been here a long time, it's a transcript -- purports to be a transcript of meetings held over the course of a full day at President Tudjman's office. I would like to reserve our argument on that or take no position on that until such time as we have a translation. We have only very small translations of selected excerpts, and it seems to me that given the parties, given the context, and given the length of time this recording covers, it would be only useful for us to have a translation to appreciate the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the meeting was just about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification for the time being, and we'll decide -- make our determination after having heard from Ms. Edgerton. We give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1143, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As regards the intentions of the Serb side, you had quite a few beliefs and quite a few impressions, but what you did know was -- well, let us focus on what you did know. In paragraphs 35 through 39, and 56 through 59, you spoke about peace plans, and you repeated a few times that Serbs wanted peace, but on their own terms; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes. I haven't looked at my statement, but, yes, I know that that's something that I had said and was reflected in my statement somewhere, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 19 in the statement, and then 35 through 39, and 56 through 59, state what it was that we wanted; negotiations, plans, and so on. At one point, you said that we wanted more than 50 per cent of Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I believe that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you attend any one of these conferences during the war?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Sorry. Which conferences?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Peace conferences, those that discussed the peace plan that was supposed to be adopted.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I never attended any formal international peace conferences for Bosnia. I was present in many Contact Group meetings or meetings of Contact Group representatives and other meetings with senior officials of the parties, where peace talks or elements of a peace agreement were discussed. But in terms of an international conference, I don't -- there was the -- there were hardly any conferences that took place by the time I got there, so, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that we accepted, very early on, that we would agree to less than 50 per cent? For example, at the very start, at the Lisbon Conference, we accepted that we would have 44 per cent. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also, during the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, we accepted that the Muslims would have 33.5 per cent and the Croats 35.7 -- or, rather, 17.5, which would make up 51 per cent altogether?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly look at 65 ter 17686. This is a letter dated the 8th of July, 1994. It's from the Secretary-General, and it's addressed to the president of the Security Council. It has to do with plans. Now, can we look at page 12, please. Actually, page 13 in e-court. I would kindly ask all the participants to have a look at this. I'm going to read it in English: [In English] "In paragraph 12 of the report submitted to the Security Council on 29th of December, 1993, by the co-chairmen of the Steering Committee (S/26922), the stage which peacemaking efforts in respect of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina had reached was summarised as follows:" [Interpretation] And now this is what it says here: that there's going to be a union of three republics, Bosnia would be a union of three republics; and the Muslim-majority republic would have 33.3 per cent, and the Croats would have 17.5 per cent. And then look further on; that this republic would have access to the sea, and the discussions between Silajdzic and Krajisnik would continue on territorial delimitation. And then 46 says that on the 18th and 19th of January, a map was proposed by the Bosnian Serbs, offering the Muslim-majority republic 33.56 per cent, while the Bosnian Croats would get 17.5 per cent. And Izetbegovic made it known that that was what they had been offered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you not see that the Muslim side also wanted to have access to the sea, and they thought they were entitled to it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that the Bosnian Government authorities, the authorities in Sarajevo, wanted access to the sea, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that Lord Owen said in public - we even have the recording somewhere here - that this was the first time that an army which was not defeated would cede such a large territory; it was not defeated, but for the sake of peace, it was willing to cede such big territory, so from 70 per cent to 49 per cent?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I am not familiar, offhand, with Lord Owen's statement to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document, which originates from the UN, be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just so that the record is straight, this is not a letter that has to do with plans, as Dr. Karadzic said. It's the report of the co-chairmen of the Steering Committee of the activities of the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Right. Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1144, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As we can see, the conference was continuing. Do you agree that there was not a single day when some conference or other was not ongoing? If I may remind you, in late 1991 and early 1992, the Cutileiro -- or, rather, the Carrington-Cutileiro Conference started, and it was ongoing until the 22nd of August, 1992, when Owen and Stoltenberg took over -- or, rather, they took over in late 1993. And then in early 1994 -- or, rather, in spring 1994, it was the Contact Group Plan, and finally there was the Dayton Agreement. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I agree that there were those distinct processes that were undertaken in pursuit of peace in Bosnia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I suppose you agree that before the war and without the war, the European Community, as it was then called, used mediators, such as Carrington and Cutileiro, and proposed through them three ethnic republics in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is known as the Lisbon Agreement or the Cutileiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I'm vaguely familiar with that plan. I was not working on Bosnia issues, as I indicated, until April 1994. Upon starting that work, I did familiarise myself with agreements that -- prior agreements or discussions that had a significant impact on the current-day events, April 1994 and afterwards events, but I'm not an expert on what happened politically before that period.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For your information, all three sides accepted this agreement, and had the Muslims not rejected it later on, there would have been no war and we would have had less than 49 per cent. But you can see that in the United Nations document. Can we now please see --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is there a question? Is there a question about all three sides accepting this agreement; you know, what Dr. Karadzic has just offered to us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, refrain from making statements, or put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can just add a question mark at the end, because Mr. Banbury continued to carry out certain duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So did you know that on the 18th of March, 1992, all three sides had accepted the Lisbon Agreement, and a week later the Muslim side rejected it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I wouldn't have known the exact dates, but I was generally aware of those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now please see 1D3424. Let us please focus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, we agree that this is the 6th of June, 1994. It's a telegram from Ambassador Akashi to Stoltenberg, Annan and himself. Please have a look at item 2. Please read for yourself what is in the frame, item 2 and the beginning of item 3, and also item 4, with the three sub-items. When you have read it, please tell us so that we could move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I've completed reading it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Once again, please focus just on what is encircled, though you're not limited to that. Would you agree that in item 5, it says in brackets that the Muslims do not want UNPROFOR inter-positioned between the sides and that -- were you aware of this Serbian proposal, and was it justified and reasonable, from a military point of view, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I confirm the document says that the Muslims do not want UNPROFOR interpositioned. I am aware of this discussion, this proposal. As to whether it was reasonable or not, I think that question has to be answered in context, in terms of what was implementable and not implementable, what was going to be acceptable by other parties, what wasn't going to be acceptable. It has to be looked at in a broader context, as opposed to the -- just the elements, the individual elements. Certainly, some of the elements are very reasonable, in my view, and would have been helpful had they been -- had they been agreed by all sides and respected by all sides. Others were probably not going to be accepted. And as a result, they -- this was -- this was a proposal by one side that was not going to be accepted by the other side, but it was a basis on which UNPROFOR could perhaps conduct some negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the first part of item 7, where Karadzic and Krajisnik advocate that even if the agreement was unsuccessful, that the arrangements for Sarajevo should remain because they might help to preserve peace in Sarajevo. Would you agree that this is noted here as the proposal made by Krajisnik and Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I agree there's reference to separate arrangements for Sarajevo. I think there were many times when you and Bosnian Serb authorities made proposals for Sarajevo, for the airport, for the safe areas, for UNPROFOR movements that were wholly unacceptable from the UN perspective, so I don't know what the elements of the special annex might have been. The principle sounds good. Whether it makes sense or not or is reasonable depends on the specific elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that when you enter negotiations, you first come out with the highest price and then later on you might relent?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that's standard practice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1145, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll stay with this topic for yet a while, the negotiations, and what Republika Srpska or the Serbian side wanted, so can we please have 1D3425.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have noted that the Serbian side was not in favour of short cease-fires, and sometimes the reasons why we were not in favour of short-term cease-fires was not really properly understood. Can you please have a look at item 3 here. These were negotiations, as you can see, concerning the cessation of hostilities, which were held in Geneva. Do you remember that in the video-clip, I said that truces are one thing and the cessation of hostilities is something else which we request because it's an introduction for peace? Would you agree that cessation of hostilities is something much more extensive and much wider between the sides and warring parties than a simple truce?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, in principle, that should be the case, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that the Serbian side had certain reserves when it came to a cease-fire that would last only four weeks, and was it clear to you that it was much work to do and then after four weeks the fighting might break out again, and would you agree that this was a good reason not to accept such a proposal as delineated in item 3?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I agree that a cessation of hostilities agreement required a lot of work and commitment by the parties and UNPROFOR, and was a very significant event to occur and, ideally, last longer than four weeks, reasons for rejecting it, in general, by whomever could vary, and they may have a range of reasons. Some, they may publicly state; others, they may not. I was of the view that an important consideration in the decision by you and your authorities not to accept a short-term cessation of hostilities was that it allowed the -- your opponents to perhaps gather strength, and you were interested in locking in territorial gains that you had already achieved. That was my assessment. Whether you also had the motivation that you just suggested is something I can't confirm. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that we have said publicly what is the first part of your claim. But as for the other part, which is your belief, I think that we always accepted that we would have less than 50 per cent. Would you agree that we have just seen that much earlier, it was something that had already been accepted?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: There, you and your authorities had accepted that you might -- that you might get less than 50 per cent of the territory, but that -- an individual element of a peace agreement can't be looked at by itself. It needs to be looked at in the broader context of the entirety of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please see the next page. The whole page can be important to read, but item 4 says that the Serbian side, on the other hand, agreed to our proposed duration of four months. This is what the UN proposed, four months, for the cessation of hostilities; that we accepted also the proposed arrangement on the separation of forces and withdrawal and control of heavy weapons; and so on. And item 5: [In English] "However, when we informed the Bosnian Serb side of the positions insisted upon by the Federation side, none of the Federation proposals were acceptable to them. The Serb side stated that the maximum they can compromise is to agree on the four-month cessation of hostilities, as proposed by the seven ministers and by the UN." "Seven ministers" means 7G -- G7: "Dr. Karadzic said that if the Federation side wishes to discuss a cease-fire, it should be done under an entirely different framework. He emphasised that his side was co-operative and made considerable compromise during this round of negotiations ..." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. And now everyone can have a look at everything else, but can we now please also see the last page so that it would be seen that, in the end, we accepted this and agreed to the four weeks. Ambassador Akashi was someone we could not resist, and we made many concessions. Please see that in a month, they would agree not to engage in any offensive military operation or provocative actions. And it was signed by Nikola Koljevic, Ejub Ganic. I don't know who it was on behalf of the Croats who signed it. And Ambassador Akashi signed it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do the Serbs sound as if they were acting cooperatively, judging by this document?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can it be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1146, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
