utterances.text: Your Honour, this is -- the cross-examination with respect to this document has been little more than having the witness confirm what the document actually says, and I have a hard time accepting that Dr. Karadzic might need more time when he uses the time that he has, in large passages, to have the witness confirm what's printed on a document that could be dealt with by way of written argument.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My main question was whether the Serbian side was co-operative, in terms of implementing a cease-fire, if not the cessation of hostilities. The witness has looked at the document and confirmed this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, actually, Dr. Karadzic, the witness only confirmed what the document appeared to say. He didn't confirm any facts flowing from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, the Chamber is of the view that these documents are relevant to understand the context of the witness's evidence. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honour, maybe it was not properly translated. I asked the witness, Does the sound as if the Serbs were co-operative, on the basis of this document? And the witness confirmed, he said, Yes. Perhaps there was a problem with the translation. Can we now please see 1D2456.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness's answer was noted -- reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a telegram also sent by Akashi to Annan and the UN. The date is the 21st of June, 1994. This is in the midst of negotiations, not just negotiations about the peace plan proposed by the Contact Group, but also negotiations concerning a cease-fire or, rather, cessation of hostilities. Please focus on item 1: [In English] "Immediately following the effective date of the 8th of June, 1994, Geneva Agreement on the cessation of offensive activity, UNPROFOR noted a significant decrease in the level of activity on BiH and BSA confrontation line." [Interpretation] And further on, anyone can read. Please have a look at item 2: [In English] "The majority of both direct and indirect fire violations have been initiated by the BiH, particularly in, but not restricted to, the Sector North-East area of responsibility." [Interpretation] Is this in line with what we've been saying all along, that it was them who violated the cease-fires and placed us in an impossible position? And in connection with important events, that is to say, conferences, did we also inform you about this, as confirmed here by Ambassador Akashi?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I believe that UNPROFOR -- that the information on which Mr. Akashi is reporting these events to UN headquarters in New York is most likely -- most likely from UNPROFOR military reporting or UN Military Observer reporting and not just based on information from the Bosnian Serbs. In this case, in this particular instance in June 1994, it was the -- and in the days after the Geneva Agreement, it was the Bosnian Government military that was responsible or that was taking -- had the greater share of responsibility for violating the cease-fire in this particular case, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, in any event, that Ambassador Akashi would not rely only on our protests, but exclusively relied on UN sources. Can you please look at paragraph 3 now. Second sentence, it says: [In English] "It seems to reflect a lack of Bosnian Government will to implement the agreement and may even be an indication of somewhat dubious motives on their part in signing it." [Interpretation] And then 4: [In English] "In addition, you will recall from UNPROFOR Z-840 [sic] of June 18th, 1994, that it has been the BiH authorities who have demonstrated the least co-operation in moving forward on the second aspect of the Geneva Agreement: the immediate and complete release of all persons detained, including -- persons detained, including prisoners of war." [Interpretation] And then down there in the 5: [In English] "I am particularly concerned that failure on our part to denounce its continued violations on the part of BiH, is likely to bring about - as was the case in the past - a disproportionate counter-offensive by the BSA. Accordingly, I would request that these disturbing events be brought to the attention of the Security Council. I have attached a draft presidential statement on the subject, which may be of assistance to you." [Interpretation] And the last page is a draft how Ambassador Akashi believes that the president's statement should look like. Mr. Banbury, do you see that Mr. Akashi is completely aware that keeping silent about Muslim violations of the agreement was dangerous because it would lead to a disproportionate counter-offensive by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I think this reporting is very clear. Mr. Akashi was accurately conveying to United Nations headquarters in New York our best understanding of the situation on the ground, the developments, and the responsible party. I think what this document very clearly shows is a lack of bias on the part of UNPROFOR in reporting events on the ground, a lack of partiality in terms of favouring or supporting or being against one side or the other. We accurately reported what was happening on the ground, our understanding of who was responsible, and our recommendations on how to promote a peaceful course of action. And that was a commitment and a practice to which UNPROFOR was strongly attached throughout, I think, the history of the peacekeeping operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we agree, in part, well, let's look at page 2, where it does, nevertheless, say that: [In English] "I am particularly concerned that failure on our part to denounce its continued violations on the part of the BiH ..." [Interpretation] Thus, the Muslim side wasn't even warned in time, neither was this announced, and that was the gist of our objection regarding partiality, because the Muslim side in that way believed that they can do whatever they wanted. Do you agree that Ambassador Akashi, himself, says that this must stop and that this party must -- all right, well, if you can just look at paragraph 5, then. Would you agree that it indicates that up until then, there were omissions in publishing such cases?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I do not believe that's what that paragraph refers to. The paragraph clearly states at the beginning that UNPROFOR will continue to raise these issues with the Bosnian Government. We very often raised, at the highest levels with President Izetbegovic, with his prime minister, with other senior military and civilian officials, their responsibilities and cases where they were violating Security Council resolutions or undertakings that they had made, formal or informal. We brought that to their attention and insisted that they respect them. The paragraph later says that: "... failure on our part to denounce its continued violation on the part of the BiH is likely to bring about - as was the case in the past - a disproportionate counter-offensive ..." So the concern is that there would be a disproportionate counter-offensive by the Bosnian Serb Army, and hence that there needed to be more decisive action than UNPROFOR raising it with the Bosnian Government. And that course of action being recommended by Mr. Akashi was a presidential statement, so I think it's a -- it's a logical sequence of events. We were trying to resolve the situation on the ground. We didn't believe that our efforts on the ground were likely to achieve the desired result, and hence there was a recommendation to the -- to UN headquarters in New York that action be taken at the Security Council level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then am I correct in saying that this does not refer to the actions towards the Muslim side, but it's directed at informing the public and the actions by the Security Council? It says that it was not announced before, and seeks that the Security Council be informed about it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Yes, my reading of the paragraph suggests that if we do not take action at the New York level, the Security Council level, then the response by the Bosnian Serb Army to the violations of the agreement by the Bosnian Government Army is going to be as it was in the past, a disproportionate counter-offensive.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we admit this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1147, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3423 so that we can see that General Mladic is pursuing the same logic when, some two or three weeks before that, he addresses Boutros-Ghali and the De Lapresle Command. And General Rose, this is his letter, which was sent up along the UN lines, and now he says: [In English] "I wish to draw your attention to successive and increasing Muslim violations of the cease-fire in the area of Sarajevo carried out with different weapons and, as a rule, against the civilian objects and population." [Interpretation] And then he cites examples. And then in paragraph 2, he says: [In English] "On 24th of May, 1994, against the same region, a civil bus on the route Hadzici-Subotica was shot. One woman was killed, whilst 13 passengers, mostly women, were wounded, two of them seriously." [Interpretation] Can we have the following page. We can see the whole page, and then he says -- now General Mladic is posing questions. Let's look at 2, for example: [In English] "I am disappointed by UNPROFOR impossibility and unpreparedness to undertake effective and proper measures. Why does UNPROFOR undertake no effective measures towards the Muslims to stop the mentioned armed and other offensive activities?" [Interpretation] And then a sentence a little bit lower: [In English] "... why the world bodies and public are not informed of obvious anti-peaceful behaviour of the Muslims?" [Interpretation] And that is now a letter signed by Milovanovic, as the chief of Mladic's staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this comport with what Ambassador Akashi, himself, says; that not everyone is informed about these violations?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: Well, I note that this letter is from General Milovanovic and is not a UN document, so the incidents that were -- are alleged to have taken place in the letter, I don't know if they were ever confirmed by the United Nations. And with all due respect, we did not rely on information by any one side on which to report to UN headquarters in New York. We sought to confirm, as best as possible, information through a variety of means. So I don't know if those events took place. And if they did, I don't know to what extent we may have reported on them either to UN headquarters -- we also, as a very routine matter, had press conferences -- daily press briefings in Sarajevo where major or significant military events were reported to the world's press, and I believe we sought to report factually and accurately and fairly and impartially the events that were taking place on the ground; not just to UN headquarters in New York, but to the world that was paying close attention, and we did that, in part, through those daily press briefings. In terms of the questions asked by General Milovanovic in this paragraph 2, why UNPROFOR doesn't take any effective measures toward the Muslims to stop the offensive activities, why are they not obliged to adhere to what is agreed, regrettably, with great regret, UNPROFOR was not able to oblige any party to respect the agreements that they had voluntarily undertaken, or other international obligations that they may have had flowing from Security Council resolutions or international agreements, and we could not compel parties to stop fighting or to cease their activities. That was very much the case with all the parties, and it was extremely unfortunate that we weren't able to and that the parties didn't respect their obligations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In the context of the Akashi telegram, could we admit this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Banbury, but you would not deny that UNPROFOR received such letters at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we routinely received such types of letters and protests from the Bosnian Serbs, or really all sides were, as a regular practice, passing on what they claimed were information about facts or events on the ground and complaining to us about our failure to act to prevent incidents against their populations. This was quite routine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1148, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D3428, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, I would like to remind you that both Mladic -- actually, Milovanovic, on behalf of Mladic, and Akashi said that the public was not sufficiently informed and that there was a kind of [indiscernible]. And now we're going to show you why this happened, why the public was not informed. This is a telegram of the 22nd of July of 1994 about the visit of the state secretary for defence, William Perry, to our zone. Can we have page 3 of this document, please. Could you look at page 3, the framed highlighted areas, where Secretary Perry states three possible courses of action to open the plan of the Contact Group: [In English] "First, the group could de-emphasise disincentives, citing practical difficulties, and rely on long-term economic and diplomatic pressure with no essential change of UNPROFOR's role. We replied that UNPROFOR could not expect to be unaffected by any form of increased pressure on the Serbs, but that isolation was an effective tool. "Secondly, Secretary Perry stated that the group could choose rigorous enforcement of exclusion zones, accepting the need for UNPROFOR to withdraw. Secretary Perry stated that this option would 'look like a war and force us to think and deploy forces that way, helping the Bosniaks and perhaps the Croats against the Serbs.'" [Interpretation] And then a little bit lower, you can look. I will begin: [In English] "At the same time, we could seek a constitutional arrangement that while failing -- while falling short of granting international recognition would provide the Serbs a large degree of autonomy and dignity, as well as rights to confederation similar to those enjoyed by the Croats." [Interpretation] Mr. Banbury, would you agree that what was being contemplated here was also the defeat of the Serbs, with giving support to Muslims and Croats to defeat the Serbs, and would you agree that the actual plan of the Contact Group did not provide for autonomy and dignity, and that that would be something that would need to be thought about, autonomy and dignity to the Serbs, and that this was something that needed to be considered?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: My view of those options were they were being presented by Secretary Perry in a theoretical sense, the theoretical options available to the international community. But as -- I agree, and it's noted there at the top of the paragraph currently on display on the page, that none of the options cited -- well, there, it says "worked well." They weren't very feasible. There was little willingness on the part of the international community or NATO to go to war in Bosnia, and so they needed to come up with a -- in this case, a fourth course of action, and that fourth course of action explicitly suggests that there needed to be a way to provide Serbs with a large degree of autonomy and dignity. So I guess, I'm sorry, I don't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did see up in that part that enforcement -- an enforcement zone was being mentioned, and do you remember that at the time our weaponry were being monitored by the UNPROFOR in the 20-kilometre exclusion zone? It was already under supervision, and the international community, via the United Nations, was planning to step up measures against the Serbs, looking towards their defeat, and: [In English] "We could seek a constitutional arrangement that, while falling short of granting international recognition, would provide the Serbs with a large degree of autonomy and dignity." [Interpretation] So this is thus a reserve option for which we had to fight for with our persistence and sacrifice, and we had already handed over our weaponry to the United Nations; isn't that right? The exclusion zone was already in force, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: But, Dr. Karadzic, it wasn't respected by your military authorities. There were widespread violations by the Bosnian Serb Army of the heavy weapons exclusion zone around Sarajevo. You had heavy weapons scattered throughout the zone. Even the heavy weapons that the Bosnian Serb Army had placed in weapons collection points were still controlled by the Bosnian Serb Army, monitored by UNPROFOR but controlled by the Bosnian Serb Army. And subsequent events during the course of the war, when the Bosnian Serb Army withdrew the weapons from the collection points and used them against your enemies showed clearly that the weapons were not under UNPROFOR's control. And the option that you referred to in this document here about enforcing the weapons exclusion zone: One, it was simply stating that an option was being considered to enforce decisions that had already been taken regarding obligations that the Bosnian Serb Army had or the Bosnian Serb authorities, and that those obligations were not being respected in terms of the presence of heavy weapons in the exclusion zone. And the option of enforcing respect for the weapons exclusion zone and enforcing your authority's adherence to them was rejected because it would have been a too high level of conflict for the international community, so Secretary Perry -- and it seems the UN was ruling out the possibility of using force to enforce your -- the obligations that you were -- the obligations you had, but you were not respecting. So, I'm sorry, I have a very different reading of this document than you do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to see how that actually looks. Can we admit this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1149, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D3426, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, I would just like to ask you this: Did you know that we did have the right to take our weapons back in certain circumstances and use it in our defence?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I do not believe that was the case. And if it were the case in some very limited circumstances, certainly the conditions that would have, in theory, allowed you to take the weapons and use them in self-defence were, from the UNPROFOR view, never met when you -- when you took those weapons out and used them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomorrow, we're going to show, hour by hour, how much we restrained ourselves. But let's look at the dispatch by General De Lapresle on the 16th of June, 1994, status of the Sarajevo Exclusion Zone. Paragraph 1: [In English] "I have attached a list of the BSA uncontrolled weapons within the Sarajevo Exclusion Zone." [Interpretation] Anybody can read this. Can we look at item three now, at the bottom, please: [In English] "The perception which may exist in certain quarters that UNPROFOR is not in control of the 20-kilometre zone is false. A number of the weapons listed are inoperable. Most others are visited regularly or are under UNPROFOR observation. In addition, many of the weapons in violation do not have sufficient range to reach Sarajevo. Allegations made which assert that the Serbs regularly remove weapons from the WCPs are false and must be refuted."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a response to the impression that you gained most probably from the Muslim press?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: My impression and UNPROFOR's understanding of the situation in the heavy weapons exclusion zone was based on information we collected ourselves, not at all upon whatever press outlets may have said. We did have observers -- military observers who were able to, at times, observe some weapons. We did have personnel based at the weapons collection points. We had access to aerial photography. It was through a variety of sources that we developed our understanding of the presence of Bosnian Serb Army weapons -- heavy weapons in the exclusion zone. It is the case, as is indicated in this paragraph 3, that some weapons were under our direct observation. It is the case that some weapons were in weapons collection points, where we were present. It is the case that some weapons were old and rusty or of limited range. While those are, indeed, facts, it is also the case that there was a persistent pattern of violation of the heavy weapons exclusion zone by the Bosnian Serb Army, with numerous placements of heavy weapons within the zone, some of which could reach and were used against the civilian population of Sarajevo. The UNPROFOR leadership routinely brought these concerns to the attention of yourself and the Bosnian military leadership, and we were never, ever, throughout the course of the war, satisfied with the response, because the heavy weapons exclusion zone regime was never fully respected, and this became a critical element in the final days of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will get to that tomorrow. You will see how things stand there. Can we admit this? And one more document before we finish, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1150, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 17724, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that we didn't want to adopt the Contact Group Plan. You said the Serb side refused. But if you hadn't known, now we will see that it was a question of a semantic trap and splitting of the hairs on the side of the international community. This is a telegram, the weekly situation report of the 1st of May, 1995, and then it says: [In English] "Bosnian parties refuse to extend Carter's [indiscernible] Contact Group for being bogged down in semantics." [Interpretation] Can we now look at the following page, please? Actually, two pages on. In paragraph 57, you call that plan a reasonable one. But if we look at paragraph 10 here, I'm going to read it: [In English] "Former US President Carter, in a television programme which was joined by Dr. Karadzic by a satellite link on 4th of May, berated the Contact Group for missing the opportunity to negotiate peace in Bosnia by letting negotiations devolve into a squabble over semantics. Peace, Carter contended, had been held hostage by the Contact Group's insistence that the Serbs should accept the Contact Group Plan before direct talks between the parties could begin. Carter appealed to 'all forces that are now interested in that area (to) focus their attempt to induce, even to force, both parties to co-operate in a good-faith peace effort - without preconditions ...'" [Interpretation] And so on. So President Carter understood that we were requested to say we the Contact Group plan, and then we'll negotiate. But what were we to negotiate if we would accept the plan? And President Carter understood that the issue was the word "accept," instead of "we agree," and so on, that this was the semantic trick which was really without much value as compared to the opportunity to establish peace. Would you agree that President Carter, himself, believes that the Serbs were not to blame for this?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY BANBURY
utterances.text: I had the privilege of being assigned by Mr. Akashi to accompany President Carter as an UNPROFOR political advisor when President Carter engaged in the peace talks in Bosnia in December of 1994, and I was able to spend the three or so days that he was in Bosnia with him, including in all the talks he conducted with you, Dr. Karadzic. And so I have great respect for President Carter and think he played a very valuable role in December 1994. In May of 1995, or really after December 1994, including up through May 1995, he wasn't intimately engaged in the peace process any longer. And I think he was very committed to peace in Bosnia, with the best of intentions, but I'm not sure that he had inside knowledge of what the Contact Group was doing and why they were perhaps pursuing the course of action they were pursuing. So, yes, he -- it's clearly conveyed in the document, President Carter's views, but I think there was a reason the Contact Group, with all the different representatives of all the different countries, had their opinion why that condition was a necessary one to pursue the peace process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1151, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that will be it for today. We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of March, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.34 p.m.,
